## 59. MoE with CPU offload: routed experts on the CPU, everything dense on the GPU, streamed prefill (2026-11-20)

Branch `perf/offload-r1` (base `develop` at `9b341bb8`). GPU 0 of the RunPod machine (RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell 32 GB, no resizable
BAR), AMD EPYC 7443 (Zen 3: AVX2 + FMA, no AVX-512 / VNNI) with a ~10-core cgroup quota and 62 GB of memory, llama.cpp b11177 (CUDA
and Vulkan builds). The GPU was shared with another perf agent (runs serialized with a lock) and the CPU with a model-feed build job
and that agent's vLLM: decode numbers moved by 10-20 % between runs of one build (`cpu.stat` throttled 15 % of the periods); the
tables give best / median of 64 steps, and the medians of "before" and "after" ran under comparable load. Sharplight: `sharplight
<model> --provider cuda|vulkan --cpu-offload --bench 512` (prefill best of 5 warm 512-token passes, decode 64 steps after them).
llama.cpp: `llama-bench -ngl 99 -ncmoe N -fa 1 -p 512 -n 64 -r 3 -t 10` (mean of 3), N swept, the best shown.

### 59.1 What the time went to (before)

Qwen3.5-122B-A10B UD-IQ2_XXS (36.6 GB) with `--cpu-offload` placed whole layers: 43 of 50 groups on the GPU, the last 6 layers
and the output head on the CPU. A decode step took 38.4 ms: 8.4 ms on the GPU and 30 ms on the CPU, of which the 248320 x 3072 Q4_K
output head (0.43 GB read every token) took 8.5 ms, the dense attention / delta-rule / shared-expert projections of the 6 layers 9 ms
and the routed experts 11 ms (the float dequantize path at ~12 GB/s). A 512-token prefill spent 2.3 of its 2.4 s on the CPU.
llama.cpp with `-ncmoe 6` (the experts of 6 layers on the CPU, the rest on the GPU) decoded at 72 tok/s; the 21.5 tok/s of
docs/model-support.md was its layer split (`-ngl 38`).

### 59.2 Changes

* **Expert placement** (`PlacementPlanner`): with a CPU fallback the routed experts of a layer (the `MatMulId`s over a bank with more
  experts than a token selects, the activation between them and the weighted sum over the k slots) are a placement group of their own;
  when the model does not fit, the experts of the first layers go to the CPU, as few as needed, and attention, shared experts, dense
  layers and the output head stay on the GPU. Only the normed hidden rows, the ids and the slot weights go to the CPU and one summed row
  per token comes back. The planner keeps room for those transfer buffers, a segment's own overhead and the graph outputs
  (`ReservePerSegment`). `PlacementOptions.SplitExperts`, `SHARPLIGHT_SPLIT_EXPERTS=0` for the old layer split.
* **Shared activation arenas** (CUDA, Vulkan): the segments of one model on a device run one after another and now share their
  transient buffers, so 20 segments do not hold 20 arenas (170-280 MiB each at 512 rows).
* **CPU expert kernels**: `MatMulId` takes the integer-dot path (8-bit activations, as `MatMul`), with decoders for the IQ2 / IQ3 grid
  formats and fused AVX2 dots for them (grid magnitudes times sign-flipped activations with `vpmaddubsw`, one sign-table lookup per
  eight values, `vpsignb`): IQ2_XXS 2.80 ns and IQ2_S 3.67 ns per 32 values on one core; per decode call (8 experts, 1024 x 3072)
  0.53 → ~0.3 ms (IQ2_XXS) and 0.79 → ~0.37 ms (IQ2_S). Experts with more than four rows in a pass keep the float path (it reuses a
  dequantized tile over the rows). Other tiers decode and dot as before; MXFP4 / K-quants use their existing integer-dot decoders.
* **Streamed prefill**: from 32 rows per pass (`StreamExpertsMinRows`) the CPU experts run on the GPU instead, their weights copied in
  for each pass into one layer's worth of memory the placement keeps free (`CompileOptions.StreamWeights`; the streamed segments of a
  model share it). On CUDA the mapped pages of the streamed weights are page-locked read-only (within the pinned-memory limit, else a
  quarter of the process memory) and copied asynchronously while the GPU runs the layer before (`IStreamedSegment.BeginStreaming`):
  0.67 GB per layer at 28 GB/s; a staged copy (one pair of staging buffers per device) reached 14 GB/s. Vulkan copies through staging
  on a worker thread (23 GB/s). A streamed compilation that does not fit leaves its layer on the CPU.

### 59.3 Qwen3.5-122B-A10B UD-IQ2_XXS (tok/s, best / median)

| | CPU groups | decode | prefill 512 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| CUDA before (layer split) | 7 (6 layers + head) | 26.0 / 25.5 | 211 / 207 |
| CUDA, experts on the CPU, no streaming (`SHARPLIGHT_STREAM_EXPERTS_MIN_ROWS=0`) | 8 | **58.4 / 57.6** | 227 / 222 |
| CUDA, experts on the CPU + streamed prefill (default) | 10 | 53.1 / 52.2 | **927 / 926** |
| llama.cpp CUDA `-ncmoe 6` / `8` | | 72.1 / 65.2 | 985 / 866 |
| llama.cpp CUDA `-ngl 38` (layer split) | | 9.2 (shared GPU) / 21.5 (§ model-support) | 589 |
| Vulkan before (layer split, `develop`) | 10 | 15.6 / 8.3 (GPU shared during part of the run) | 142 / 140 |
| Vulkan, experts on the CPU + streamed prefill | 14 | **43.5 / 42.8** | **705 / 688** |
| llama.cpp Vulkan `-ncmoe 6` / `8` | | 44.7 / 40.2 | 751 / 643 |

* Decode 2.0-2.2x on CUDA, 2.8x on Vulkan (17.8 in docs/model-support.md); prefill 4.4x on CUDA, 5.0x on Vulkan. Against llama.cpp:
  CUDA decode 0.74x (0.81x without streaming), prefill 0.94x; Vulkan decode 0.97x, prefill 0.94x. The CUDA rows are the final build
  (develop merged), run while the machine was otherwise quiet; earlier runs of the same placement under load gave 47-51 tok/s.
* The CUDA decode step of the default build: GPU 9.6 ms (llama.cpp's whole step is 13.9 ms) and ~1 ms per CPU expert layer. The GPU
  part is ~1350 launches over 48 layers (the largest projections stream at ~720 GB/s, the rest are small kernels); llama.cpp fits 42
  expert layers where this placement fits 38-40: the 1 GiB device reserve, the 512-row logits buffer (485 MiB), the streaming buffer
  (0.67 GB) and the per-segment buffers take ~2.5 GiB. Vulkan budgets 92 % of the device and fits 3 GiB less.
* Greedy output: the FamilyGenerationTests cases (raw prompt, chat turn, story; 32 tokens against llama.cpp b11177) pass on CUDA and
  Vulkan with the new placement.

### 59.4 gpt-oss-120b MXFP4 (ggml-org GGUF, 63.4 GB; tok/s, best / median)

36 layers of 128 experts (top 4) with biases, MXFP4 experts of 1.69 GB per layer. On the CPU the MXFP4 experts use a fused AVX2 dot
(codes looked up as signed doubled E2M1 values with `vpshufb`, |w| times the sign-applied activations): 1.58 ns per 32 values against
3.06 ns for decode + dot. The CUDA MXFP4 expert layout is repacked, so its streamed copies go through staging (0.56 GB per layer in
~27 ms); the file is 1.4 GB larger than the cgroup's memory, so the CPU's share is read from the page cache with some eviction (llama.cpp's
prefill varies by ±40 % between its three runs).

| | CPU expert layers | decode | prefill 512 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| CUDA, first build of this branch (bias gathers split from their experts: ~190 segments) | 23 | 25.4 / 24.9 | 203 / 189 |
| CUDA (default) | 20 | **48.1 / 47.5** | **278 / 232** |
| llama.cpp CUDA `-ncmoe 20` / `22` / `24` | | 36.0 / 40.4 / 32.5 | 137 / 176 / 107 |
| Vulkan (default) | 22 | **44.1 / 43.0** | 71 / 63 |
| llama.cpp Vulkan `-ncmoe 22` | | 34.8 | 107 |

* CUDA decode 1.19x and prefill 1.6x of llama.cpp's best setting; Vulkan decode 1.27x, prefill 0.66x.
* Vulkan prefill is bound by the streamed copies: 1.7 GB per layer in ~370 ms median (207 ms at best). Vulkan budgets less of the GPU, so
  36 GB of experts stay on the CPU and are re-read for every pass; with the 63 GB file in a 62 GB cgroup part of them comes from disk
  each time (the CUDA placement keeps 33 GB on the CPU and copies a layer in ~100 ms). Repacking MXFP4 into cached memory before the
  write-combined staging buffer (this branch) cut the worst copies but not the median.
* Greedy text (`-p "The capital of France is" -n 32`): CUDA and Vulkan identical to each other and to `develop` (layer split, float CPU
  experts): " Paris.\n\nGreat! If you have any more questions ..."; llama.cpp b11177 (CUDA, `-ncmoe 22`) repeats " Paris." after the
  first sentence, so the difference predates this branch.

### 59.5 Tests, what did not work, and what limits it

| suite | result |
|---|---|
| Sharplight.Cpu.Tests (incl. new PlacementExpertTests, IntDot IQ / MXFP4 decoders and fused dots, MatMulId integer dots and pairs) | 1358 / 0 failed / 36 skipped |
| Sharplight.Vulkan.Tests affected classes on CUDA and on Vulkan (StateHandoff, StreamedExperts, Moe, RowInvariance, QuantFormat, F16Range), one class per process | 419 / 0 failed each |
| Sharplight.Cuda.Tests | 27 / 0 failed / 1 skipped |
| FamilyGenerationTests, Qwen3.5-122B-A10B UD-IQ2_XXS (3 cases against llama.cpp), CUDA and Vulkan, after merging `develop` | 3 / 0 each |
| gpt-oss-120b greedy text, CUDA and Vulkan against `develop` | identical |


* The plain integer-dot path (decode a row into codes, then the generic dot) was slower than the float path for IQ2_XXS (0.66 against
  0.53 ms per decode call): the per-16 scale and offset arithmetic outweighs the 8-bit products. The fused dots replaced it; an AVX2
  gather of the grid entries (`vpgatherqq`) was slower than scalar loads (4.58 against 2.81 ns per 32 values); IQ2_S gained nothing from
  the one-lookup sign table (it reads explicit sign bytes).
* Pairing the gate and up products into one op (one quantization, one pass) is in (bit-identical results), but its effect on the decode
  step was within the run-to-run noise of this machine.
* Two streaming memories (`SHARPLIGHT_STREAM_BUFFERS=2`, the next layer's copy overlapping the current layer) made the 122B prefill
  slower, 831 against 927 tok/s, and decode 47.8 against 53.1: the extra layer of experts it moves to the CPU costs more in each pass than
  the overlap saves. It stays an option, off by default.
* A thread-count sweep (8 / 10 / default threads) was inconclusive: other jobs took 2-5 cores during most runs.
* Copies through staging buffers reached 14 GB/s on CUDA (17 GB/s with the MXFP4 repack) against 28 GB/s from page-locked mapped
  memory; on Vulkan the repack wrote out of order into write-combined staging memory (5 GB/s) until it went through cached memory first.
* Decode on CUDA stays behind llama.cpp: the GPU part of a step (9.5 ms) and three to four more expert layers on the CPU. Each moved
  layer costs a GPU segment boundary, a transfer buffer and the per-segment reserve; streaming costs one layer's memory (~10 % decode for
  a 4.5x faster prefill; `SHARPLIGHT_STREAM_EXPERTS_MIN_ROWS=0` keeps it for decode-only use).

### 59.6 Reproduce

```bash
export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=<i> SHARPLIGHT_VK_DEVICES=<i> GGML_VK_VISIBLE_DEVICES=<i>
CLI=samples/Sharplight.Cli/bin/Release/net11.0/sharplight
M=~/models/gguf/Qwen3.5-122B-A10B/Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-UD-IQ2_XXS.gguf     # or gpt-oss-120b/gpt-oss-120b-MXFP4.gguf
for p in cuda vulkan; do SHARPLIGHT_LOAD_TIMING=1 $CLI $M --provider $p --cpu-offload --bench 512; done
SHARPLIGHT_STREAM_EXPERTS_MIN_ROWS=0 $CLI $M --provider cuda --cpu-offload --bench 512    # no streamed prefill (more GPU room)
SHARPLIGHT_STREAM_BUFFERS=2 $CLI $M --provider cuda --cpu-offload --bench 512             # two streaming memories
SHARPLIGHT_SPLIT_EXPERTS=0 $CLI $M --provider cuda --cpu-offload --bench 512              # whole layers on the CPU (before)
SHARPLIGHT_CPU_PROFILE=1 SHARPLIGHT_CUDA_PROFILE=1 $CLI $M --provider cuda --cpu-offload --bench 64
for n in 6 8; do $LLAMA_ROOT/runtime.llama-b11177-cuda13/llama-bench -m $M -ngl 99 -ncmoe $n -fa 1 -p 512 -n 64 -r 3 -t 10; done
HOME=<model mirror> SHARPLIGHT_TEST_LARGE=1 SHARPLIGHT_TEST_CUDA=1 SHARPLIGHT_TEST_CASE="Qwen3.5-122B-A10B UD-IQ2_XXS" \
  dotnet run --project tests/Sharplight.Families.Tests -c Release -- -method "*Generation_matches_reference_on_cuda"

## 60. Serving round 1: a serving step profile, asynchronous executions, window-sized KV caches (2026-11-20)

Branch `perf/serving-r1` (base `develop` at `f3d279f0`). GPU 0 of the RunPod machine (RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell), shared with other agents:
every timed run held the verify lock and `QUIET_GPU=1` repeated rounds during which another process computed on the GPU. vLLM 0.33.0
(same venv as §56-58), rerun in this session. Raw output in [`bench/results/s60/`](../bench/results/s60).

### 60.1 Where a 64-stream serving round goes

`SHARPLIGHT_STEP_PROFILE=<file>` (new, `StepProfiler`) writes one CSV line per engine step: rows, the scheduler thread's phases (admission,
scheduling, the decoder's packing / upload / run / read-back, result processing, GC pauses) and the device time of the step
(`ICompiledSegment.LastRunTimings`, new: GPU ms, host record / submit / wait ms, recorded or replayed). The gap between two steps' starts minus
the device time is the time the GPU waited for the host. `bench/s60_steps.py` summarizes a file. gpt-oss-20b, `bench/s16_serve.sh` at
64 streams (64 slots of 512 tokens, ~250-token prompts, 128 output tokens), one round (192 requests), excluding the gaps between
rounds. "develop-equivalent" is this branch with `SHARPLIGHT_ASYNC_EMIT=0`: the CUDA execution returns at submission, but the decoder
reads its results at once, so the host waits exactly where `develop` waited.

| | steps | rows (decode + prompt) | period ms | GPU ms | GPU idle ms | host phases while the GPU waits (ms) |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| **develop-equivalent**, decode-only steps | 489 | 48 + 0 | 16.71 | 15.59 | 1.12 (p50 at 64 rows 0.19) | schedule 0.01, pack 0.05, upload 0.02, submit 0.14, process (sampling, stop checks, detokenization, streaming) 0.15 |
| mixed (prompt-wave) steps | 35 | 40 + 1400 | 109.6 | 96.3 | 13.2 | admission 0.93, schedule 0.35, pack 1.05, record 2.46 + launch 1.88 (a new row count: no graph), process 1.32 |
| whole round | 524 | | 22.91 | 20.98 | 1.93 (8.4 %) | |
| **this branch**, decode-only steps | 490 | 48 + 0 | 16.16 | 15.83 | 0.32 (p50 at 64 rows 0.14) | process work runs during the next step (overlap 0.03 ms) |
| mixed steps | 34 | 41 + 1441 | 105.3 | 99.5 | 5.9 | (record not yet overlapped in this run, see 60.2) |
| whole round | 524 | | 21.94 | 21.26 | 0.68 (3.1 %) | |

* The round is GPU-bound: the GPU is busy 91.6 % (develop-equivalent) and 96.9 % (this branch) of the time. Prompts arrive in waves (the
  closed-loop clients finish together), so prompt rows come as ~8 steps of up to 2048 rows per wave, not as a few rows in every step.
* Device time per step: a decode-only step of 64 rows costs 18.7 ms GPU (p50 over 1,056 serving steps), of 16 rows 11.9 ms. Prompt rows
  add 57.8 µs each (least-squares fit over the steps with ≥ 48 decode rows: 19.6 ms + 57.8 µs per prompt row). vLLM's inter-token latency
  p50 at 64 streams is 12.9-13.3 ms against our 18.7-19.0, so vLLM's decode steps at ~54 running sequences take ~13 ms: **the serving gap
  is device time of the decode steps and of the prompt rows, not host time** (median GPU idle between replayed decode steps 0.14 ms,
  graph launch to first kernel included).
* GC: 37-40 ms of pauses in a whole Qwen3-8B-FP8 16 + 64-stream run (1,172 steps, no generation-2 collection, at most 11 ms; `gc_pause_ms`
  column), and 40 ms in a 6-second 64-stream run of a tiny model on the CPU (the same HTTP / SSE load per token). A handful of 50-80 ms stalls in the GPU runs (read-back far longer than the
  step's GPU time, 73 of ~4,000 steps, ~5 % of a 16-stream round) coincide with neither GC nor recording; they look like the scheduler
  thread being descheduled on the shared host (model-feed build).
* Per-token streaming work (detokenization, stop strings, the channel write that wakes the SSE writer) is 0.1-0.15 ms per step at 64
  streams; the JSON per chunk is written on the request's thread, not the scheduler's.

Mixed-step kernels (`BatchBench --mixed`, CUDA profile, ms per step; 64 decode rows at depth 256 + one 107-row prompt against 64 rows alone):

| | 64 rows | 64 + 107 rows | |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| whole step (GPU, min of 10) | 18.41 | 25.07 | +62 µs per prompt row |
| expert gate / up | 9.04 (skinny `gemm_sk`) | 10.38 (`gemm_moe_native`) | the grouped MXFP4 GEMM leaves the skinny form above 64 rows; at ~21 rows per expert it is not at the read limit |
| expert down | 3.64 (skinny) | 5.79 (native) | |
| q / k / v / o (`gemm_cm2` split-K) | 2.44 | 3.64 | |
| decode attention | 1.28 | 1.81 | |
| prefill attention (`attn_prefill_native`) | | 0.56 | |

So the prompt-row cost of a mixed step is mostly the expert GEMMs (3.5 of 6.7 ms), which belong to the kernel work of perf/llm-r15
(GEMM kernels and their selection were out of scope for this round).

### 60.2 Asynchronous executions and step preparation

* `ICompiledSegment.ExecutesAsynchronously` (new) / `CompiledModel.RunsAsynchronously`: the CUDA and Vulkan segments return from `Execute`
  once the work is submitted. A segment waits for its own execution before it reads an output, takes an input, copies state, resets or
  runs again; on CUDA also before another segment of the device runs (`CudaDevice.Pending`: forwarded inputs and borrowed states).
  Profiled executions, data-dependent counts and submission budgets keep waiting at once. `LastGpuMs` / `LastRunTimings` wait first.
* The engine uses the window between submission and read-back (`MultiSequenceDecoder.WhileRunning`): tokens whose text cannot end the
  sequence (no stop strings, no log-probabilities, no constraint) are committed at once (stop tokens, lengths, the next input) and
  detokenized and streamed while the next step runs (`InferenceEngine.FlushEmits`; a sequence's deferred tokens are flushed before it
  completes). `SHARPLIGHT_ASYNC_EMIT=0` turns it off. Provider-neutral: a provider whose executions wait (CPU, Metal) streams at once.
* A shape's first run (mixed steps of a new row count) is launched launch by launch while it is recorded, so the GPU starts after the
  first launch instead of after ~700 launches have been resolved, and the CUDA recorder no longer runs the Vulkan hazard tracking
  (one stream needs no barriers). Mixed-step GPU idle 5.9 → 1.7 ms (record 3.1 → 1.0 ms, now overlapped with the GPU).
* What was not built: scheduling step N+1 before step N's tokens are known (vLLM's async scheduling, which feeds sampled tokens to the
  next step on the device). With the GPU busy 97 % of a round after the changes above, it could gain at most the remaining ~3 %; the
  serving gap is device time (60.1).

gpt-oss-20b serving (two rounds each, mean; aggregate output tok/s / TTFT p50 ms / mean inter-token latency ms; "before" =
`SHARPLIGHT_ASYNC_EMIT=0 SHARPLIGHT_DISABLE_FEATURES=window_kv` on the same build, run right after "after"):

| streams | before | **after** | vLLM | CUDA / vLLM before → after |
|---:|---|---|---|---:|
| 16 | 1138 / 110 / 13.1 | **1141 / 111 / 13.1** | 1424 / 183 / 9.9 | 0.80 → **0.80** |
| 64 | 2381 / 255 / 23.8 | **2395 / 266 / 23.6** | 3154 / 413 / 17.0 | 0.75 → **0.76** |

Qwen3-8B-FP8 (no window layers), `SHARPLIGHT_ASYNC_EMIT=0` / `=1` alternated twice, one round each, mean (vLLM: §58.4, same machine):

| streams | emission at once | **overlapped** | vLLM | CUDA / vLLM (§58.4 → now) |
|---:|---|---|---|---:|
| 16 | 988 / 115 / 15.3 | **991 / 119 / 15.2** | 1115 / 168 / 12.9 | 0.87 → **0.89** |
| 64 | 2440 / 276 / 23.5 | **2447 / 287 / 23.4** | 2691 / 400 / 20.2 | 0.87 → **0.91** |

(A first Qwen pair in a busier slot measured 730 / 2206 against 964 / 2358 tok/s with a 640-tok/s round, rounds 22 % apart; the
alternated pairs above agree within 0.5 % and replace it. Both variants include the asynchronous executions and the overlapped first
recordings; against §58.4's 974 / 2345 on `develop` they are +1.7 % / +4.4 %.)

The earlier single-round pair of 60.1 measured 2330 → 2410 tok/s (+3.4 %); across the session our rounds spread by ±2 %, so the gain
of the host-side work is 0.5-3 %, as its share of the round predicts.

### 60.3 Window-sized KV caches

gpt-oss-20b alternates full layers and layers that attend to the last 128 keys; until now both kept a row per position of the paged
pool. Window-sized caches ([kv-cache.md 2.8](kv-cache.md#28-window-sized-caches-for-sliding-window-layers-implemented-the-default),
`window_kv`, on by default) keep only the blocks each slot's window reaches, in a pool of their own with a second block table; the
attention and cache-write kernels are the paged forms already used, so CPU, Vulkan, CUDA and Metal run them unchanged. Prefix caching
(window blocks stay cached under the main blocks' hashes), forks, follower prefixes, truncation by rejected drafts (64-position margin),
preemption and attention sinks (gpt-oss's are a per-head logit, not cached positions) work as before.

| gpt-oss-20b KV cache (f16) | full layers | window layers | total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 4 streams x 131,584 positions, before | 12.05 GiB | 12.05 GiB | 24.09 GiB (+ 12.8 GiB weights: does not fit in 32 GB) |
| **after** | 12.05 GiB | **0.07 GiB** (3,008 rows) | **12.12 GiB** (fits) |
| 64 slots x 512 (serving), before | 0.75 GiB | 0.75 GiB | 1.50 GiB |
| **after** | 0.75 GiB | 0.40 GiB (17,408 rows) | 1.15 GiB |

The pool is sized so it never runs out (slots x (window + margin + 3 blocks) + one step's rows), so its share shrinks as contexts
grow; `EstimateFootprint` / `KvBytesPerToken` count it at that size, so hosted models fit more context, or more slots, in the same memory.

Decode at long depth (`BatchBench --slots 4 --ctx D+512 --depth D --batch 2048`, GPU ms per step, tok/s; vLLM as §58.8):

| depth | 1 stream CUDA / vLLM | 2 streams | **4 streams CUDA / vLLM** |
|---:|---|---|---|
| 32,768 | 6.43 ms: 155.5 / 150.7 tok/s (1.03) | 8.54 ms: 234 tok/s | 13.29 ms: 301 / 310.8 tok/s (0.97) |
| ~128K | 10.04 ms: 99.6 / 107.3 (0.93) | 15.63 ms: 128 tok/s | **26.88 ms: 148.8 / 174.9 tok/s (0.85)**, did not fit before |

Trade-off with prefix caching. The window pool is sized for the running slots, so window blocks that left a window are evicted much
sooner than main blocks, and a cached prefix can only be attached while the window blocks at its end are still cached. Vulkan, gpt-oss-20b,
64 streams (one round each, two alternated pairs; "off" = `SHARPLIGHT_DISABLE_FEATURES=window_kv SHARPLIGHT_ASYNC_EMIT=0`): the load
generator repeats the prompts of the 16-stream round (same seeds), and with full-length window caches 16 of 192 prompts attached a
cached prefix (3,840 of 48,003 prompt tokens), with window-sized caches none:

| Vulkan, gpt-oss-20b | 16 streams | 64 streams | cached prompt tokens (64) |
|---|---|---|---:|
| `window_kv` off | 1234 / 138 / 11.8 | 2311 / 365 / 24.3 | 3,840 |
| **on** (default) | **1241 / 139 / 11.7** | **2255 / 326 / 24.6** (-2.4 %) | 0 |

Conversation turns that return to their slot keep their window blocks (the slot holds them), and recently finished prompts' blocks are the
last evicted, so chat-style reuse is unaffected; reuse of prompts seen hundreds of requests earlier is not. The remedy is vLLM's layout,
one block pool for both groups, so window blocks compete for eviction with full blocks instead of with each other (not built: it changes the
pool accounting of admission and preemption). `window_kv` can be disabled where long-lived shared prefixes matter more than memory.

Correctness: the window layers read the same K / V values through another table, so outputs are bit-identical:
`WindowKvParityTests` (tiny random Cohere2 MoE GGUF / HF and Gemma 4 MoE, 8-key windows, 40-token outputs after prompts of 45-70 tokens,
sequential and concurrent prompts with prefix hits, forks of three samples) is token-identical with and without `window_kv` on CPU,
Vulkan and CUDA; `WindowKvCacheTests` checks every query's window rows through the window table in the engine's paged scenarios
(prefix hits, forks, preemption, speculative drafts, a small shared pool).

### 60.4 Mixed-step budget and chunk size

gpt-oss-20b, 64 streams, one round each (aggregate tok/s / TTFT p50 ms / mean ITL ms); defaults: step budget 32 rows per running
sequence within 768-2048 rows (§50), chunks of the whole budget. vLLM 0.33.0 runs with its default chunked prefill and
`max_num_batched_tokens=8192`.

| setting | tok/s | TTFT p50 | ITL |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| defaults (60.2, mean of two rounds) | 2395 | 266 | 23.6 |
| `--step-tokens 1024` | 2324 (-3 %) | **182** | 24.6 |
| `--min-step-tokens 0` (always the full budget) | 2439 (+1.8 %) | 281 | 23.2 |
| `--prefill-chunk 512` | 2430 (+1.5 %) | 262 | 23.3 |
| `--step-tokens 4096` (capped at the 2048 compiled rows) | 2399 | 264 | 23.4 |

Prompt rows cost the same per row at every step size (57-62 µs from 107 to 2048 rows, 60.1), so the budget only moves time between TTFT
and inter-token latency: smaller steps stream first tokens sooner at a small throughput cost, and no setting moves throughput beyond the
±2 % spread of rounds. The defaults stay; our TTFT p50 is already below vLLM's (266 against 413 ms at 64 streams, 111 against 183 at 16).

## 61. LLM round 15: decode-step projections and expert GEMMs, the native f16 GEMM with a bias store (2026-11-20)

Branch `perf/llm-r15` (base `develop` at `f3d279f0`, `develop` at `120cdcb8` merged before the final runs). GPU 0 of the RunPod machine
(RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell, 82 SMs, 200 W), shared with other agents: every timed run held the verify lock and started without another
compute process on the GPU. "Before" is this branch with `SHARPLIGHT_MULTI_GEMM=0 SHARPLIGHT_NATIVE_GEMM_BIAS=0
SHARPLIGHT_CUDA_MIN_BLOCKS=none` (the kernels and launches of `develop`), alternated with "after" in the same session. vLLM figures are
those of §56-58 and §60 (vLLM 0.33.0, same machine and checkpoints). Raw output in [`bench/results/s61/`](../bench/results/s61).

### 61.1 Decode step (BatchBench `--slots 64 --ctx 512 --depth 256 --modes greedy --reps 20`, GPU ms per step, mean of two runs' minima)

| model | provider | before 1 / 16 / 64 sequences | **after** | vLLM at 64 | ours / vLLM at 64 before → after |
|---|---|---|---|---:|---:|
| gpt-oss-20b | CUDA | 5.34 / 11.89 / 17.79 | **5.34 / 10.06 / 16.12** | ~16.2 | 0.91 → **1.00** |
| Qwen3-8B-FP8 | CUDA | 11.33 / 13.43 / 17.39 | **11.33 / 13.42 / 16.92** | 15.6 | 0.90 → **0.92** |
| gpt-oss-20b | Vulkan | 5.33 / 9.93 / 17.26 | 5.32 / 9.92 / 17.21 | | |
| Qwen3-8B-FP8 | Vulkan | 11.18 / 13.50 / 17.25 | 11.19 / 13.53 / 17.28 | | |

What changed, by size of the effect:

* **Launch bounds for the expert-grouped skinny GEMMs (CUDA)**: gpt-oss-20b at 16 / 64 sequences -1.83 / -1.53 ms. 61.2.
* **Multi-output q / k / v GEMM**: gpt-oss-20b -0.17 ms and Qwen3-8B-FP8 -0.45 ms at 64 sequences. 61.3.
* The fused split-K reduction (in the GEMM's last workgroup) was built and measured slower; it is opt-in (61.4).

### 61.2 The expert-grouped skinny GEMM on CUDA: launch bounds

Profiled side by side (`--profile`, gpt-oss-20b, minimum per launch), the skinny MXFP4 expert GEMMs were slower in their CUDA form than
in their SPIR-V form: at 16 sequences gate / up 108.5 against 67.4 µs, down 47.3 against 42.8 µs, and the whole CUDA step 12.0 against
10.0 ms on Vulkan (64 sequences: 17.5 against 16.7 ms). NVRTC / ptxas gave the dual kernel 160 registers without spills for its 128
threads. Stating the block size and one resident block per SM (`__launch_bounds__(128, 1)`, added by the CUDA translator to the
`gemm_sk` entries of the MoE sources, `NvrtcTranslator.DefaultMinBlocks`) changes how ptxas schedules the weight stream:

| `__launch_bounds__(128, n)` on the MoE skinny GEMMs (gpt-oss-20b, GPU ms per step, 16 / 64 sequences) | |
|---|---|
| none (before) | 12.04 / 17.69 |
| n = 1 | **10.05 / 16.22** |
| n = 2 | 10.15 / 16.29 |
| n = 4 (≤ 128 registers) | 12.75 / 21.55 |
| n = 5 | 17.11 / 32.51 |
| n = 2 on every `gemm_sk` (also the dense skinny GEMMs and the LM head) | 10.06 / 16.28; Qwen3-8B-FP8 13.66 / 17.04 (+0.2 ms at 16) |

So the bounds stay on the expert kernels only. `SHARPLIGHT_CUDA_MIN_BLOCKS=file:entry:blocks[;...]` (or `none`) replaces the default and
is part of the translator's cache key; the translator options version is 6 (cached PTX of version 5 is recompiled). Bounds change only
ptxas's register allocation and scheduling, not the arithmetic: greedy outputs are byte-identical (61.6).

At 64 sequences the step is now at vLLM's (16.12 against ~16.2 ms). The coordinator's finding from §60 (the grouped MXFP4 GEMM below the
read limit at ~21 rows per expert in mixed steps) was measured but not solved: 64-row native tiles (`SHARPLIGHT_NATIVE_MOE_SHORT=48` /
`96`, new), 128-row weight tiles (`SHARPLIGHT_NATIVE_MOE_BN=128`, new), the skinny GEMM up to 24 items per expert
(`SHARPLIGHT_MOE_SKINNY=24`) and the native GEMM from 24 items per expert all cost 0.1-1.6 ms per 64 + 107-row step (`s3/`, `s4/`).

### 61.3 Multi-output q / k / v GEMM

Sibling matmuls that read the same activations with weights of one format and K (`FindMultiGemmGroups`: q / k / v, all with a bias row or
none, at most one width that is not a multiple of 128, placed last) keep their own launches and, at the batches where each of them splits
K (9-256 rows), are served by one GEMM over the concatenated weight rows instead (`EmitMultiGemm`, splitk.slang `MULTI`): each matrix
stays its own buffer, a tile's weight base is chosen by its first row (every tile reads one matrix), and the split-K reduction stores each
column into its member's output with its bias. Nothing in the `.slm` layout or the uploaders changes. Both families: gemm_cm2 (16-bit and
other generated formats) and the fp8 GEMM (an fp8 matmul splits K on gemm_cm2 at 9-16 rows and on the fp8 GEMM from 17 rows, so a group
gets one multi-output GEMM per family).

| per layer at 64 sequences (CUDA profile, minimum µs) | before | **after** |
|---|---|---|
| gpt-oss-20b q / k / v (bf16 as f16, biases) | 35.0 + 9.0 + 9.0 + 3 x 1.8 reductions = 58.4 | **41.4 + 3.9 = 45.3** (one split-K GEMM [2880 → 4096 + 512 + 512], 712 GB/s, and one reduction) |
| Qwen3-8B-FP8 q / k / v | 28.6 + 10.4 + 10.4 + 3 x 2.1 = 55.7 | **40.9 + 4.0 = 44.9** |

* The 512- and 1024-row k / v matrices ran 4-8 column tiles each, split 8-16 ways; in the concatenation they share the 40-48 column
  tiles of q. Each output sums its K slices in the concatenation's split order, so where that split differs from the member's own split
  the partial sums round differently (as between any two split counts); greedy outputs are byte-identical on the prompts of 61.6.
* Vulkan: the fp8 form is used (Qwen3-8B-FP8 at 64 sequences 17.25 → 17.28 / 17.09 in two pairs: neutral), the gemm_cm2 form only on
  CUDA C++ targets, because on the NVIDIA Vulkan driver gpt-oss-20b's 64-sequence step lost 2.5 % with it (16.85 → 17.28 ms).
* `SHARPLIGHT_MULTI_GEMM=0` disables it; `SHARPLIGHT_MULTI_DEBUG=1` reports groups that got no GEMM and why.

### 61.4 Split-K reduction in the GEMM's last workgroup (built, measured slower, opt-in)

`splitk.slang`: the workgroups of a tile write their partial slices, publish them (device-scope release) and count their arrival in a
per-tile counter; the last one acquires the slices, sums them in slice order (bit-identical to `splitk_reduce`) and stores the result with
the epilogue, then resets the counter. Forms for gemm_cm2 (with its `MM_EPI` epilogues and row-ranged copies), the fp8 GEMM and the dual fp8
GEMM, and for the multi-output GEMM. GPU µs per launch at 64 sequences (CUDA profile, minimum):

| GEMM | split | separate reduction | **fused** |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| gpt-oss o [4096 → 2880] | 8 | 39.2 + 1.8 | 46.4 |
| gpt-oss q [2880 → 4096] +bias | 4 | 35.0 + 1.8 | 42.3 |
| gpt-oss k / v [2880 → 512] +bias | 16 | 9.0 + 1.8 | 14.4 |
| gpt-oss router [2880 → 32] +bias | 16+ | 5.8 + 3.5 | 9.2 |
| Qwen3 q / o [4096 → 4096] (fp8) | 4 | 28.6 + 2.1 | 32.0 |
| Qwen3 k / v [4096 → 1024] (fp8) | 8 | 10.4 + 2.1 | 14.2 |
| Qwen3 down [12288 → 4096] (fp8) | 4 | 75.1 + 2.1 | 77.8 |
| multi-output q / k / v, gpt-oss | 4 | 41.4 + 3.9 | 49.0 |

The last workgroup of each tile reads all its slices alone (k / v: 16 slices of 32 KB per tile), at the bandwidth of one SM, at the end
of the launch, where the separate reduction spreads the same reads over the whole GPU; graph-replayed launches leave ~0.2 µs between
kernels (§58.3), so the saved launch is worth less than the tail. Whole steps at 64 sequences: gpt-oss-20b 17.80 → 18.26 ms, Qwen3-8B-FP8
17.27 → 17.80 ms. `SHARPLIGHT_SPLITK_FUSED=1` (single GEMMs) and `SHARPLIGHT_MULTI_FUSED=1` (the multi-output GEMM) switch it on.
On the NVIDIA Vulkan driver the fused fp8 GEMM returned a few wrong outputs in `FusionTests.SiblingProjections` (gemm_cm2's passed), so
the fp8 form is used only on CUDA C++ targets; an atomic through a dereferenced pointer (`InterlockedAdd(*ptr, ...)`) also never counted
there, so the counters are indexed. Two related experiments, also opt-in and slower: a K split chosen by wave fill for one-token-row grids
(`SHARPLIGHT_SPLIT_FILL=1`: gpt-oss o 39.2 → 49.3 µs; the 64-row gemm_cm2 tiles run two workgroups per SM, so the 82-tile wave it assumes
is wrong) and a K-split dual fp8 gate / up GEMM at decode sizes (`SHARPLIGHT_FP8_DUAL_SPLIT=1`: Qwen3-8B-FP8 step 17.3 → 22.6 ms).

### 61.5 gpt-oss prefill: the native f16 GEMM with a bias store

`gemm_f16_native.cu` takes `H_BIAS` (the store adds the bias row) and `H_XRS` (the rows of a row-ranged f16 copy are multiplied by
their inverse scale first, exact, as the unscale launch did), so q / k / v / o with biases leave gemm_cm2 (`UseNativeBiasGemm`, from 1024
rows: at 256-512 rows gemm_cm2's split-K reduction with the bias epilogue was faster).

| | before | **after** |
|---|---:|---:|
| gpt-oss-20b prefill 512 / 2048 / 8192 tokens (tok/s, best of the `--bench` runs) | 13,203 / 15,770 / 14,594 | 12,923 / **16,132 / 14,865** (512: unchanged path, noise) |
| ours / vLLM (11,436 / 16,379 / 15,812) | 1.15 / 0.96 / 0.92 | 1.13 / **0.98 / 0.94** |
| mixed step 64 + 960 rows (ms) | 74.57 | **73.73** |
| Qwen3-8B-FP8 prefill 512 / 2048 / 8192 (no biases: unchanged) | 14,459 / 14,207 / 11,747 | 14,492 / 14,159 / 11,730 |

Not done: the expert gather / slot sum fused into the routing and the down GEMM (§58.9 lever 4b). The gather of the gate / up input could
be done on load by the native MoE GEMM (indexed `cp.async` rows of an unsorted f16 copy), but the larger part is the down projection's
gather of the gate / up output, which needs the dual GEMM to store its f16 output in sorted order with the range guard of an unbounded
product (a fix-up pass like `f16_range_fixup`); a fused slot sum by atomics would make the outputs depend on the order of arrival.

### 61.6 Correctness and tests

* Greedy text, 120 tokens, the round's features on and off (CUDA): Qwen3-8B-FP8 byte-identical after a short, a ~170-token and a
  ~1000-token prompt; gpt-oss-20b byte-identical after the short and ~170-token prompts. After the ~1000-token prompt (prefill rows on the
  native bias GEMM) it diverges ~300 characters into the answer, a near-tie as in §58.6 (a different f16 GEMM sums in another order).
  The launch bounds alone leave it byte-identical.
* New tests: `FusionTests.SiblingProjections` (q / k / v of 1024 / 256 / 136 rows over K = 1536 with and without biases, bf16 / f16 /
  q8_0 / E4M3 weights at 16-300 rows: the multi-output GEMM, its last member unaligned, and the batches it does not serve) and a 1100-row
  `FusionTests.MatMulBias` case (the native bias GEMM). The sibling test also passes with `SHARPLIGHT_MULTI_FUSED=1` and
  `SHARPLIGHT_SPLITK_FUSED=1` on CUDA.

|---|---:|---|
| gpt-oss-20b decode step, 64 sequences | **1.00** (16.12 against ~16.2 ms) | expert GEMMs ~10.2, projections 2.6 (q / k / v 45 + o 41 µs per layer), attention ~1.3 |
| Qwen3-8B-FP8 decode step, 64 sequences | 0.92 (16.92 against 15.6 ms) | FP8 gate / up dual GEMM 147.5 µs per layer at ~680 GB/s (192 workgroups at one per SM: 2.3 waves), down 75, q / k / v 45, o 31 |
| gpt-oss-20b serving 16 / 64 streams | 0.91 / 0.80 | 64: mixed steps (prompt rows ~60 µs each; the grouped MXFP4 GEMM at 16-48 rows per expert below the read limit) |
| Qwen3-8B-FP8 serving 16 / 64 streams | 0.89 / 0.89 | its decode step |
| gpt-oss-20b prefill 512 / 2048 / 8192 | 1.13 / 0.98 / 0.94 | experts and attention ahead at 2048; expert gather + slot sum 7.5 against 1.5 ms per pass; norms / rope ~9 ms |
| Qwen3-8B-FP8 prefill 512 / 2048 / 8192 | 1.05 / 0.95 / 0.95 | FP8 GEMM main loop at 76 % of the MMA peak per cycle against CUTLASS's ~90 % (§57.2) |
| long prefill 16K-128K | 0.92-0.94 (gpt-oss), 0.93-1.00 (Qwen3) | attention 9-15 % behind FlashInfer at 128K |
| long decode, 1 / 4 streams | 0.92-1.03 / 0.90-1.09 | decode attention at depth |

Ranked levers:

1. **Mixed-step expert GEMMs** (gpt-oss serving at 64 streams, 0.80x): the grouped MXFP4 GEMM at 16-48 rows per expert (§60.1: 3.5 of
   the 6.7 ms a 107-row prompt adds); 64-row tiles, narrower tiles and the skinny form were measured slower (61.2). Candidates: split K
   over two blocks per tile at these sizes (more blocks per SM and a stream that reaches the read limit), or the skinny form's
   register-direct fetch with the native kernel's `cp.async` ring.
2. **FP8 decode GEMMs at one workgroup per SM** (Qwen3 decode 0.92x): gate / up runs 192 workgroups in 2.3 waves of 82; a decode
   form with a smaller register budget or a hand-written `cp.async` skinny FP8 GEMM (CUDA), ~1.2 ms per step → ~15.7 ms.
3. **gpt-oss prefill MoE glue**: the down projection's gather of the gate / up output and the slot sum (~5 ms per 2048-row pass), see 61.5.
4. **FP8 GEMM main loop** (§57): ~+7 % Qwen3 prefill.
5. **Attention at long prompts and decode at depth** (§58.9 lever 6).

## 62. MoE with CPU offload, round 2: CPU expert layers split with the GPU, resident streamed experts, integer dots for the IQ grid formats (2026-11-20)

Branch `perf/offload-r2` (base `develop` at `fef12123`, §59 merged; `develop` merged again at `2e10734b` and `164f4ebc`, the suites below rerun after the last merge for Moe, QuantFormat, StreamedExperts, TopK and the 122B FamilyGenerationTests: all pass, CUDA decode 70.9 / 69.7, prefill 999). Same machine and methodology as
§59: GPU 0 of the RunPod machine (RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell 32 GB, no resizable BAR), AMD EPYC 7443 with a ~10-core cgroup quota (AVX2, no
AVX-512), llama.cpp b11177, the GPU shared with another perf agent (runs serialized with a lock) and the CPU with a model-feed job and that
agent's tests. Sharplight: `sharplight <model> --provider cuda|vulkan --cpu-offload --bench 512` (prefill best of 5 warm 512-token passes,
decode 64 steps; tok/s best / median); llama.cpp: `llama-bench -ngl 99 -ncmoe 6 -fa 1 -p 512 -n 64 -r 3 -t 10` (mean ± sd of 3).
`SHARPLIGHT_SEGMENT_TIMING=1` (new) prints the host time of every segment per decode step.

### 62.1 Where the decode step went (start of the round)

Qwen3.5-122B-A10B UD-IQ2_XXS on CUDA, 50.5 / 47.8 tok/s: the experts of 10 layers on the CPU (llama.cpp: 6) at ~1.2-1.5 ms each under this
machine's load, 9.5 ms on the GPU (1350 launches). The GPU's spare memory went to the 512-row logits buffer (485 MiB, a session reads one
row), the 1 GiB reserve (of which ~1.1 GiB was still free after compiling), the streaming memory (one layer's experts, unused in decode), the
`ReservePerSegment` of 32 MiB counted twice per moved layer, and activation arenas that the segments did not share (166 + 174 + 274 MiB:
each larger segment compiled later allocated its own). On the GPU, the routed experts in IQ2_XXS / IQ2_S ran the f32 expert matvec at
~370 GB/s with gate and up in separate launches; the router took five launches (softmax, top-k, sum, scale, divide).

### 62.2 Changes

* **Split CPU expert layers** (`CompiledModel.RunSplit`, `CompileOptions.SparseExpertSlots`, CUDA): every CPU layer of routed experts gets a
  third compilation for passes of up to `SHARPLIGHT_SPARSE_EXPERT_ROWS` rows (default 4), whose expert banks hold only the experts such a
  pass can select (32 of 256, 84 MB for all banks, shared by the layers). In decode the GPU takes the first slots of every row and copies the
  experts they select from the page-locked mapped file into the bank slots (the ids are rewritten to slots; ~2.6 MB per expert of this model),
  while the CPU computes the other slots (ids of -1 select no expert: `MatMulId` on the CPU gives zero rows); both outputs are sums over the
  slots and are added. The GPU's share moves by one slot after every pass toward the point where neither waits (here 5.8-6 of 8 slots); a
  split layer takes ~0.75 ms against 1.2-1.5 ms on the CPU alone. Segments qualify when every expert product reads one ids input, the
  outputs are slot sums and a pass selects at most a quarter of the bank (`SparseMinExpertsPerSlot`); weights must be memory-mapped and
  stored as is (gpt-oss's repacked MXFP4 and its bias gathers keep the CPU path). Vulkan has no sparse copies yet (`IComputeDevice.StreamsSelectedExperts`).
* **Resident streamed experts** (`IStreamedSegment.WeightsResident`): the streaming memory the GPU keeps for prefill holds the last streamed
  layer between prefills (copied at load, and the last copy of every streamed pass), so that layer runs on the GPU in decode too: streaming
  no longer costs a decode layer (`SHARPLIGHT_STREAM_RESIDENT=0` for the old behavior).
* **Memory**: a session's logits buffer holds one row (`CreateSession`, `R` = 1); the largest GPU segment of each device compiles first, so the
  others share its activation arena (274 MiB instead of 614); the streamed and sparse compilations share their input and output buffers (by
  ordinal; inputs holding graph inputs excluded), counted once by the planner, which also keeps room for the sparse banks; `ReservePerSegment`
  8 MiB (the segment's buffers are counted apart); the default device reserve with a fallback device is 512 MiB (1 GiB without). A compilation
  that runs out of memory is placed again with the measured shortfall (what the rest of the plan needed beyond the free memory, plus 64 MiB)
  kept free, up to three times, and a streamed compilation that runs out of memory now triggers that retry instead of leaving prefill on the
  CPU. With the same reserve the 122B now keeps the experts of 40 layers on the GPU (8 on the CPU, one of them resident) against 38-39.
* **Vulkan budget**: with VK_EXT_memory_budget the driver's budget is the limit; the 92 % estimate only stands in without it (2.6 GB more on this
  device: 7 CPU expert layers instead of 11).
* **Integer-dot expert matvec for the grid formats** (`mmvq.slang`, `UseIntDotExpertMatvec`): IQ2_XXS, IQ2_XS, IQ2_S, IQ3_XXS and IQ3_S expert
  banks unpack 32 values per chunk from the lattice grids into signed int8 quads (sign bits applied bytewise) for the q8-activation dot, so
  decode runs the dual gate / up launch with the activation in its store and the down product with the weighted slot sum: GPU step 9.8 → 8.7 ms.
  Dense matmuls of these formats keep the f32 kernels. `SHARPLIGHT_MMVQ_GRID=0` turns it off.
* **Router fusion** (`FuseRouterTopK`, `topk_softmax` in topk.slang): a top-k (k ≤ 16) of a softmax over [rows, experts] with the renormalization
  of the selected weights (ReduceSum, Scale, Div) runs as one subgroup launch that computes the probabilities as the softmax kernel does:
  -0.40 ms per decode step (9.02 → 8.62 ms GPU; 1011 launches for 40 layers and the head). `SHARPLIGHT_NO_ROUTER_FUSION=1` turns it off.

### 62.5 Tests, and what did not work

| suite | result |
|---|---|
| Sharplight.Cpu.Tests (incl. new `MoeTests.NoExpertIdsGiveZeroProducts`) | 1360 / 0 failed / 36 skipped |
| Sharplight.Core.Tests | 1660 / 0 failed / 331 skipped |
| Sharplight.Vulkan.Tests on CUDA and on Vulkan, one class per process: StateHandoff, StreamedExperts (new `SplitExpertsMatchTheCpu`), Moe, RowInvariance, QuantFormat (IQ grid formats now on the int-dot expert matvec), F16Range, TopK (new `Router`), Fusion | 523 / 0 failed on CUDA; 523 / 0 failed / 2 skipped on Vulkan (no sparse compilations) |
| Sharplight.Cuda.Tests | 27 / 0 failed / 1 skipped |
| FamilyGenerationTests, Qwen3.5-122B-A10B UD-IQ2_XXS (3 cases against llama.cpp), CUDA and Vulkan, after merging `develop` | 3 / 0 failed each |
| gpt-oss-120b greedy text, CUDA and Vulkan | identical to §59 |

* Tightening the reserve before the planner counted the sparse banks ran out of memory while compiling; the first retry added a fixed
  256 MiB per attempt, which moved one layer more than needed (9 against 8). Retries now reserve the measured shortfall, and the planner
  counts the banks (84 MB for 32 slots).
* A copy of selected experts that spanned the page-locked range of a weight and the pageable partial pages around it failed
  (`cuMemcpyHtoDAsync`: invalid argument); copies are split at the registered range's ends.
* Sharing the streamed compilations' input buffers broke when a graph input fed them (the caller sets graph inputs for every segment before
  a run, so the shared buffer held the last segment's): only inputs of intermediate values are shared (caught by `StreamedExpertsTests`).
* Sparse compilations for one row (`SHARPLIGHT_SPARSE_EXPERT_ROWS=1`, 21 MB of banks) measured 74.4 / 71.2 and 73.9 / 70.9 against 71.9 / 69.7
  and 72.4 / 69.9 for four rows (+1.5 %, within noise); four rows stay the default so that serving steps of 2-4 sequences split too.
* The first Vulkan run with the driver's budget had 100-300 ms per streamed layer copy (decode median 55, prefill 608) while the machine was
  loaded (load average 10.5); the repeated runs (table) copied at the usual speed.
* No sparse copies on Vulkan: its streamed copies go through staging memory on a worker thread, which would take CPU time from the CPU's share
  of the slots; importing the mapped file (VK_EXT_external_memory_host) would let the GPU read it directly.

Branch `perf/llm-r16` (base `develop` at `2e10734b`, round 15 merged). Section 62 is taken by `perf/offload-r2`. GPU 0 of the RunPod
machine (RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell, 82 SMs, 200 W), shared with other agents: every timed run held the verify lock, and before / after were
alternated in the same lock hold. "Before" is this branch with `SHARPLIGHT_NATIVE_MOE_SHORT=0 SHARPLIGHT_NATIVE_FP8_DECODE_BN=128
SHARPLIGHT_ATTN_STAGES=2` (the kernels and launches of `develop`). vLLM figures are those of §56-58 and §60 (vLLM 0.33.0, same machine
and checkpoints). Raw output in [`bench/results/s63/`](../bench/results/s63). GPU performance counters are not available on this pod
(`ERR_NVGPUCTRPERM`), so the kernel work used timing only: the `bench/s56_moe` harness, the BatchBench profile and a plain read test.

### 63.2 The grouped MXFP4 expert GEMM at 16-48 rows per expert: short tiles at two blocks per SM

The harness (`bench/s56_moe/bench_moe.cu`, now with a skew parameter, `harness.txt`) shows `gemm_moe_native.cu` flat at 128-256 tokens
(gate / up 0.512-0.563 ms, ~530 GB/s; down ~460 GB/s), against a read limit of 785 GB/s (a streaming read of the same 282 MB after the
same L2 eviction). In that range it is not compute-bound (the MMA work grows 2x, the time 10 %); it is bound by how much one 8-warp block
per SM keeps in flight. The 128-row routing tile's activation stages are mostly empty at ~21 rows per expert, so:

* **64-row tiles at two blocks per SM** (`NM_MINB`, a new `__launch_bounds__` minimum; three stages each): down 0.307 → 0.231 ms (uniform)
  and 0.307-0.326 → 0.266-0.270 ms (skewed). The dual gate / up tile of 256 weight rows does not fit twice in the 100 KB of an SM, so a
  short dual tile is narrowed to 128 weight rows (64 outputs), which fits: 0.510-0.545 → 0.492-0.506 ms skewed.
* Stages (3-6) and 32-row tiles change nothing beyond that; dropping the L2 prefetch hint (`NM_PF=0`) costs 75 %; 4-warp blocks and 128-row
  dual tiles at one block are slower.

In the engine (BatchBench `--mixed`, CUDA profile, 10 steps of 64 decode + 107 prompt rows, two alternated pairs):

| | gate / up (240 launches) | down | whole step (GPU ms) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| develop (128-row tiles) | 102.0-102.7 ms | 56.9-57.4 ms | 24.90 / 25.18 |
| 64-row tiles, 256 / 192 weight rows, one block (§61.2's `SHARPLIGHT_NATIVE_MOE_SHORT=48`) | 104.3-104.5 | 50.7-50.8 | 24.49 / 24.54 |
| **64-row tiles, two blocks, dual tiles of 128 rows (this round)** | **98.9-99.5** | **52.0-52.4** | **24.22 / 24.58** |

Up to 24 items per expert only (`NativeMoeShortItemsPerExpert`): at 64 + 192 rows (32 per expert) the short tiles cost 0.5 ms (28.72 →
29.25), at 64 + 448 they never applied. Routed items above that keep the 128-row tiles. The expert GEMMs of the 64 + 107-row step now
average 413 µs (gate / up, 87 % of the read limit if every expert is touched) and 218 µs (down, 82 %). The products and their K order
are unchanged (a tile's rows only regroup), so outputs are bit-identical; `CudaCodeTests.NativeMoeGemmMatchesTheCpu` has a 40-token case
(20 rows per expert, skewed, some experts over several short tiles). Switches: `SHARPLIGHT_NATIVE_MOE_SHORT=n` (items per expert, 0 =
off), `SHARPLIGHT_NATIVE_MOE_BLOCKS=1`.

Not tried (the measured headroom is ~13-18 % of these launches, ~1 ms of a 107-row step): split K over two blocks per tile (it needs a
reduction with the SwiGLU / router epilogue, i.e. a second pass over 2 x 684 x 5760 f32 partials), the skinny form's register fetch with a
`cp.async` ring. The full 128-row tiles are another matter: they run at 122 TFLOPS at 2048 tokens against a measured `mma.sync` f16 peak
of 236 TFLOPS (63.5).

### 63.3 The FP8 decode GEMMs: a decode form of the hand-written FP8 GEMM

At 64 sequences Qwen3-8B-FP8's fp8 GEMMs ran on `gemm_fp8.slang` (the dual gate / up 147.5 µs per layer with 192 workgroups at one per SM,
2.3 waves; down 75.3 µs + a 2.8 µs split-K reduction; o 30.1 + 2.8 µs). The hand-written FP8 GEMM (`gemm_fp8_native.cu`, until now from
65 rows) with its 64-row token tiles does not help as it is (17.06 → 17.10 ms: the same 192 blocks). With **64 weight rows per block**
(`F8N_BN`, new; four stages, 66 KB) the grid doubles, so the last wave is short:

| per layer at 64 sequences (CUDA profile, minimum µs) | before | **decode form** |
|---|---:|---:|
| gate / up dual [4096 → 2 x 12288] | 147.5 | **134.6** (748 GB/s) |
| down [12288 → 4096] | 75.3 + 2.8 | **69.4** |
| o [4096 → 4096] | 30.1 + 2.8 | **24.4** |
| q / k / v [4096 → 4096 + 1024 + 1024] | 40.6 + 2.8 (multi-output split-K GEMM) | kept (on the decode form: 24.4 + 2 x 13.7) |

Decode steps (GPU ms, off → on): 24 sequences 14.22 → 14.61, 32: 14.90 → 14.71, 48: 16.32 → 15.65, 64: 17.53 → 16.77 (one session; the
alternated pairs of 63.1: 17.20 → 16.44). So the decode form serves from 32 rows (`NativeFp8DecodeMinRows`) and only matmuls outside a
multi-output group (q / k / v stay on that GEMM); the 64-row token tiles of 65+ rows are unchanged. Each output sums its K blocks in the
same order in either GEMM, so greedy text stays byte-identical (63.6). `SHARPLIGHT_NATIVE_FP8_DECODE_BN=128` turns it off;
`CudaCodeTests.NativeFp8GemmMatchesTheCpu` has 40- and 64-row cases.

### 63.4 Prefill attention: a three-stage key / value ring at head size 128

`attn_prefill_native.cu` takes `FN_STAGES` (2 or 3): with three, two tiles are in flight while one is multiplied. At head size 128 the
block (8 warps, 64 KB at two stages) has the SM to itself and a tile's copy takes about as long as its multiplication, and the third stage
fits (96 KB): Qwen3-8B-FP8 prefill +0.5-1.0 % from 16K to 128K (63.1; at 32K two pairs 6,951 / 6,983 → 7,030 / 6,990). Head size 64 keeps
two stages (a third would leave two blocks per SM instead of three). Same arithmetic, so bit-identical. `SHARPLIGHT_ATTN_STAGES=n`.
The gap to FlashInfer at 128K (Qwen3 0.94x, gpt-oss 0.92x) stays.

### 63.5 What the numbers say about the remaining gap

* **gpt-oss serving at 64 streams (0.81x)** is not the small mixed steps: with prompt waves of up to 2048 rows, most expert tiles are full
  128-row tiles, which are compute-bound at ~52 % of the MMA peak (122 of 236 TFLOPS at 2048 tokens in the harness, 8 warps of one
  128 x 32 fragment block each, one block per SM). The same tiles carry gpt-oss prefill (MoE 52 % of a 32K prefill, §61.7). And §60.1's
  serving decode step (18.7 ms GPU at 64 rows) is 2.5 ms longer than BatchBench's (16.2 ms). A hypothesis, not measured this round: real
  text routes less uniformly than BatchBench's random tokens, so more experts see over 16 items and the skinny expert GEMM's 16-row tiles
  read them more than once.
* **Qwen3-8B-FP8 decode (0.95x)**: gate / up and down now run at 725-750 GB/s (92-96 % of 785); what is left below the read limit is the
  q / k / v group (585 GB/s) and the per-step fixed work. The LM head (f16 [4096 → 151936], 1.59 ms) is at the read limit.
* **Translator options version 6 (launch bounds, round 15)**: every PTX entry's key is the source digest (macros included) plus the
  translator `Id`, which contains the options version, and the driver-stage cubins are keyed `cubin/<that key>`. So PTX or cubins cached or
  precompiled under version 5 are never served: a model precompiled before the bump recompiles its kernels with NVRTC on first load (and a
  driver-only installation without NVRTC fails with the "needs NVRTC" error instead of loading stale code). The default launch bounds
  (`NvrtcTranslator.DefaultMinBlocks`) reach the keys only through the version, unlike `SHARPLIGHT_CUDA_MIN_BLOCKS`; their documentation
  now says that editing them needs a version bump. This round's kernel changes (`NM_MINB`, `F8N_BN`, `FN_STAGES`) are macros of the
  sources and change the digests.

* Sharplight.Cuda.Tests: 30 / 0 failed / 1 skipped (cuBLASLt not installed).
* Sharplight.Vulkan.Tests, one process per class, 22 classes (MatMul, Fp8Gemm, Fusion, DualGemm, Moe, Mmq, SkinnyGemm, MatMulEpilogue,

* Vulkan: no kernel or launch of the Vulkan provider changed (all three features are CUDA C++ forms). Decode steps at 64 sequences

### 63.7 Gap to vLLM and plan (state after this round)

| benchmark | CUDA / vLLM | where the time goes |
|---|---:|---|
| gpt-oss-20b decode step, 64 sequences | 1.00 | expert GEMMs ~10, projections 2.6, attention ~1.3 |
| Qwen3-8B-FP8 decode step, 64 sequences | 0.95 (16.44 against 15.6 ms) | gate / up 134.6 + down 69.4 + q / k / v 43.4 + o 24.4 µs per layer (36 layers: 9.9 ms), LM head 1.6, attention, norms |
| gpt-oss-20b serving 16 / 64 streams | 0.91 / 0.81 | prompt waves on full 128-row expert tiles at ~52 % of the MMA peak; serving decode steps 2.5 ms above BatchBench's |
| Qwen3-8B-FP8 serving 16 / 64 streams | 0.89 / 0.92 | its decode step; at 16 the generated fp8 GEMM below 32 rows |
| long prefill 16K-128K | 0.92-0.94 (gpt-oss), 0.94-1.01 (Qwen3) | attention behind FlashInfer at 128K; gpt-oss MoE tiles as above |
| long decode at depth, 1 / 4 streams | 0.93-1.03 / 0.89-1.08 | decode attention at 128K |

Ranked levers:

1. **Main loop of `gemm_moe_native.cu` on full tiles** (gpt-oss serving at 64 streams, gpt-oss prefill 2K-128K): 122 of 236 TFLOPS. Each warp
   owns 128 rows x 32 weight rows, so every A fragment is reloaded by all 8 warps and each block decodes its weights once but feeds only 4
   n-fragments per A load; candidates are a 2 x 4 warp layout with 64 x 64 warp tiles (A reuse 8, decode shared by 4 row fragments) and
   the decode issued a full block ahead. Needs performance counters (ask for `NVreg_RestrictProfilingToAdminUsers=0` on the host) to see
   the stall reasons instead of guessing.
2. **The serving decode step against BatchBench's** (gpt-oss 18.7 against 16.2 ms, §60.1): measure with real-text routing (BatchBench with
   prompts instead of random tokens) whether the skinny expert GEMM re-reads experts with more than 16 items; a 32-row skinny tile or the
   short native tile from 12 items per expert would cover them.
3. **Qwen3 decode below 32 rows and q / k / v** (Qwen serving at 16 streams 0.89x): a multi-output form of the FP8 decode GEMM (q / k / v at
   ~585 GB/s; 96 blocks), and a decode form whose K split fills the GPU at 16-31 rows.
4. **Attention at 128K** (both models ~0.93x): the three-stage ring gave 0.5-1 %; the rest is the per-tile softmax and the 64-key tiles
   (FlashInfer's 128-key tiles at head size 128, Q pre-scaled by log2(e)).
5. **gpt-oss prefill MoE glue** (§61.5, unchanged): the gather of the gate / up output and the slot sum.

$BB ~/models/hf/gpt-oss-20b --provider cuda --slots 68 --ctx 2560 --batch 2048 --depth 256 --sizes 16 --mixed 64+0,64+107x1,64+192x1,64+448x1 --modes greedy --reps 10 --profile 1

## 64. LLM round 17: decode steps on real routing, 32-row tiles of the grouped MXFP4 GEMM for batched decode (2026-11-21)

Branch `perf/llm-r17` (base `develop` at `164f4ebc`, round 16 merged; `develop` at `72962704` with perf/offload-r2's fused MoE router
merged in before every measurement below). GPU 0 of the RunPod machine (RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell, 82 SMs, 200 W), shared with other
agents: every timed run held the verify lock, before / after were alternated in the same lock hold. "Before" is this branch with
`SHARPLIGHT_NATIVE_MOE_MIN_ROWS=12` (`develop`'s hand-over from the skinny expert GEMM to the hand-written one; the two kernel
details of 64.4 are in both). vLLM 0.33.0 (the CUDA build of §56-60, same checkpoints), rerun in this session for the decode profiles.
Raw output in [`bench/results/s64/`](../bench/results/s64).

### 64.1 The decode-step comparison was not like for like

`bench/s54_vllm_decode_profile.py` (vLLM's figure in §61-63: "~16.2 ms at 64 sequences") lets vLLM *generate*: each step's input is
the token the previous step chose. BatchBench fed every decode step the same random token ids. The routing of MoE layers depends on
those inputs, and random ids route very differently from generated text: on gpt-oss-20b at 64 sequences the expert GEMMs took
292 + 141 µs per layer (gate / up + down, mean) with fixed random ids, 380 + 180 µs on generated tokens and 415 + 197 µs on generated
text after word prompts (the serving benchmark's prompts). BatchBench has two new options: `--feedback` (random-id prompts, the chosen
tokens fed back: vLLM's profile workload) and `--text` (prompts of random words from `bench/loadgen.py`'s vocabulary, tokens fed
back: the serving workload). `s54_vllm_decode_profile.py --words` gives vLLM the same word prompts and prints how many distinct texts the
64 sequences generated (43 / 48 of 64 on random ids / words: greedy text from such prompts often degenerates into repetitions, on both
engines).

| gpt-oss-20b, 64 sequences, decode step (GPU ms) | develop routing | vLLM (annotated step + 1.6 ms) | ours / vLLM |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| fixed random ids (BatchBench default, §61-63) | 16.11 | | (not comparable) |
| random-id prompts, tokens fed back (`--feedback`; vLLM's profile) | 19.90 | 14.72 + 1.6 = 16.3 | **0.82** |
| word prompts, tokens fed back (`--text`; serving) | 21.18 | 15.59 + 1.6 = 17.2 | **0.81** |

vLLM's annotated step range ends before the LM head and the sampler (no [2880 → 201088] GEMM in it), which our step includes; 1.6 ms is
our LM head (1.53 ms, at the read limit) plus sampling. So the decode step that §63 reported at vLLM parity is at 0.81-0.82x on the
workloads both engines see in serving. The difference is the expert GEMMs: Marlin takes 10.7 / 11.4 ms per step for both products of
24 layers (446 / 473 µs per layer), ours 13.4 / 14.7 ms (560 / 612 µs).

What limits ours: on text routing a decode step touches about 28 of 32 experts per layer (the hand-written grouped GEMM's per-layer time
in the engine, 398 µs, against 449 µs for all 32 in the harness), so the skinny expert GEMM reads ~370 MB per layer at ~600 GB/s,
76 % of the 785 GB/s read limit, where Marlin, on similar routing, is at about the limit. Tested and rejected on the way:

* the re-read hypothesis of §63.7: skewed routing gives some experts 20-40 items, which the skinny GEMM's 16-row tiles read two or
  three times. Two- and four-fragment skinny tiles (32 / 64 rows, every expert read once) are slower (64 sequences 19.4-19.5 → 19.9-20.8 / 50.0 ms
  with `--feedback`), the skinny GEMM's expert-major launch order (`SHARPLIGHT_MOE_TILE_MAJOR=1`) is equal at 64 and slower at 16-32
  sequences (`decode/text_variants.txt`, `decode/skinny_fragments_sweep.txt`). The extra L2 reads cost little; the per-byte rate is low.
* a K-tiled code layout (each 16-row group's 32 bytes per K step contiguous: 512-byte runs instead of 16 runs 1,440 bytes apart):
  11 % slower in the harness (harness.txt).

### 64.2 The hand-written grouped MXFP4 GEMM on 32-row tiles from 1 item per expert

`gemm_moe_native.cu` takes the expert products from 1 item per expert on average (32 routed items for gpt-oss: 8 sequences; was 12,
96 sequences), with a third routing tile class of 32 rows up to 12 items per expert (`NativeMoeDecodeTileRows`, the 64-row short tile
of §63 above, 128 rows from 24). The 32-row tile runs two blocks per SM with four stages, a dual gate / up tile narrowed to 128 weight
rows (twice the blocks). In the harness (uniform routing, all 32 experts, ms at 32 / 64 / 128 tokens) gate / up 0.444 / 0.449 / 0.467 on
64-row tiles → 0.408 / 0.416 / 0.432; 6 stages, 16-row tiles, 256-wide tiles and one block per SM are slower (harness.txt). In the engine
it is faster than the skinny GEMM from ~3 items per expert even though its tiles are mostly empty, because its `cp.async` ring with L2
prefetch keeps more bytes in flight per SM than the skinny GEMM's direct register loads (hand-over sweeps, `--text`, two runs each, GPU ms;
`decode/handover_sweep.txt`, `decode/handover_low2.txt`):

### 64.4 Two details of the kernel

* The scale copies take the `L2::256B` prefetch hint like the code copies (each 16-row group's scale rows are read 32 bytes per K step,
  so without it every stage waited for a fresh DRAM access): harness gate / up at 32-128 tokens -1.5 %, down -2-4 %, 2048 tokens equal.
* The E8M0 table entry's two half factors are broadcast with a half-pair move, which ptxas folds into the `.H0_H0` / `.H1_H1` operands of
  the `HMUL2`s instead of two `PRMT`s per decoded unit (152 fewer of ~4,000 instructions in the loop): sustained 2048-token gate / up
  2.39-2.42 → 2.375-2.38 ms, down 1.26 → 1.25 ms (the kernel is power-limited at full tiles, 64.7). Same values, bit-identical.

### 64.7 The full 128-row tiles are power-limited, not issue- or latency-limited

The 2048-token gate / up product (§63.5: 122 of 236 TFLOPS) was taken apart in the harness, now also in a sustained mode (`LOOP=n`:
2000 launches back to back, the SM clock sampled meanwhile; `harness/harness.txt`):

* Sustained, the launch takes 2.39-2.42 ms (cold best of 20: 2.18-2.26) at a 2235-2257 MHz SM clock and 200.0 W, the board's power
  limit. The 236 TFLOPS peak was measured with MMAs that reuse the same registers, which draw far less power; scaled to this kernel's
  clock from the 2.8-3.1 GHz boost range (an estimate: its clock was not sampled), it is ~170-190 TFLOPS, so the full tiles run at
  ~65-70 % of what the clock allows, not 52 %.
* Removing parts lowers the time only by the energy they take: no in-loop copies 2.03 ms (the clock rises to 2497 MHz at the same 200 W),
  no code copies 2.15, no activation copies 2.32, one A fragment load per block 2.27, no decode arithmetic 2.18 (stale shared data also
  switches less, so these over-state each part). Issue slots are not the limit (~170 non-MMA instructions per 64 MMAs, 2 warps per
  scheduler: ~25 % of the issue rate), and neither are barriers or copy waits (§56.3).
* 64 x 64 warp tiles (2 x 4 warps, the plan's first candidate) are slower (2.57 ms cold): with the B fragments decoded by both warp rows
  the decode work doubles and the kernel reaches 255 registers. Prefetch-hint variants on the code copies are 1-2 % slower.

So the remaining lever on full tiles is energy per MMA: fewer shared-memory bytes per MMA (the 128-row A tile is reloaded by all eight
warps: 128 bytes of `ldmatrix` per MMA), fewer decode instructions per weight, and wider column tiles (A is re-read from L2 for each of
the 23 column tiles). Since Marlin takes 3.40 ms for both products at 2048 rows against our 2.26 + 1.20 ms (§56.2), the 2K-128K prefill
gap is not in this kernel but in attention (29 % of a 32K prefill, §61.7) and the glue around the expert GEMMs.

### 64.8 Correctness and tests

* The 32-row tiles sum each output's K blocks in the order of the other native tiles and of gemm_cm2, so prompt chunks that moved from
  gemm_cm2 are bit-identical; batches that moved from the skinny GEMM (3-12 items per expert: decode steps of 24-96 gpt-oss sequences,
  prompts of 24-96 tokens) sum in another order than the skinny GEMM's four interleaved K parts. Greedy text, 120 tokens, before / after
  (`greedy/`): the ~170- and ~1000-token prompts byte-identical, the ~40-token prompt (31 tokens: 3.9 items per expert, now native)
  diverges at the 12th generated token ("... in the role of" / "... in the context of"), a near-tie: with the text up to that point
  as the prompt, the top logits are "modern" 9.325, "context" 9.321, "role" 9.261 before and "modern" 9.329, "role" 9.321, "context"
  9.281 after (`greedy/tie_*.txt`).
* Sharplight.Cuda.Tests: 31 / 0 failed / 1 skipped (cuBLASLt not installed); `CudaCodeTests.NativeMoeGemmMatchesTheCpu` has a 16-token
  case (8 items per expert on the 32-row tiles, compared with the CPU and, at rounding level, with the skinny GEMM).
* Sharplight.Vulkan.Tests, one process per class (Moe, StreamedExperts, SkinnyGemm, DualGemm, MatMul, MatMulEpilogue, Fusion,
  RowInvariance, BatchMatMul, Fp8Gemm, Mmq): CUDA provider 603 / 0 failed / 0 skipped, Vulkan provider 603 / 0 failed / 2 skipped
  (StreamedExperts) (`vulkan-tests.txt`).
* Vulkan: no Vulkan kernel or selection changed (the hand-over moves only where `nativeMoe` holds). Decode steps at 16 / 64 sequences:
  gpt-oss-20b 10.02 / 16.96 ms (fixed random ids; §63: 17.29 at 64), 13.60 / 20.97 with `--text`; Qwen3-8B-FP8 13.46 / 17.20 (§63:
  17.39). Serving 64.5.
* perf/offload-r2's fused router (softmax, top-k, renormalization in one launch) does not apply to gpt-oss, whose router takes the top-k
  of the logits first and a softmax over the four (`topk` 1.8 µs + `softmax` 2.0 µs per layer, unchanged); the merged `develop` measures
  where §63 did (decode step 16.11 against 16.20 ms with fixed random ids, serving 2556 against 2556 tok/s at 64 streams).

### 64.9 Gap to vLLM and plan (state after this round)

| benchmark | CUDA / vLLM | where the time goes |
|---|---:|---|
| gpt-oss-20b decode step, 64 sequences, generated tokens (`--feedback` / `--text`) | 0.88 / 0.88 (18.48 / 19.57 against 16.3 / 17.2 ms) | expert GEMMs ~12 ms (Marlin ~10.7-11.4), LM head 1.5, q / k / v / o 1.9, attention 1.3 |
| gpt-oss-20b decode step, 64 sequences, fixed random ids (§61-63's figure) | (14.57 ms; vLLM not measured on this workload) | |
| Qwen3-8B-FP8 decode step, 64 sequences | 0.94 (16.64 against 15.6 ms) | unchanged (§63.7) |
| gpt-oss-20b serving 16 / 64 streams | 0.92 / **0.86** | prompt waves on full tiles (power-limited, 64.7), decode steps as above |
| Qwen3-8B-FP8 serving 16 / 64 streams | 0.89 / 0.91 | its decode step; at 16 the generated fp8 GEMM below 32 rows |
| long prefill 16K-128K | 0.92-0.94 (gpt-oss), 0.94-1.01 (Qwen3, §63) | attention (29 % of a gpt-oss 32K prefill, 53 % of Qwen3's); gpt-oss MoE per 2048-row pass about at Marlin's |
| long decode at depth, 1 / 4 streams | 0.93-1.04 / 0.89-1.08 | decode attention at 128K |

Ranked levers:

1. **Expert GEMMs of the decode step at the read limit** (gpt-oss decode 0.88x, serving at 64 streams): both expert kernels read
   ~600-670 GB/s at decode sizes (the native one in the harness, all experts: 670 GB/s), Marlin about 785. The copy-only form of the
   native kernel is just as slow (0.442 against 0.449 ms), and a plain `cp.async` ring over the same layout reaches 728-790 GB/s with
   32-128 bytes per row and stage (`bench/s56_moe/read_pattern.cu`), so the loss is in how the kernel issues its copies (not measured
   apart yet; suspects: two dependent routing reads before a block's first copy, the E8M0 table built first, 32 bytes per row and
   stage with a barrier each, the separate scale and activation copies). Candidates: a
   decode-only form with 64-128 bytes of codes per row and stage (the activation stage is a few rows), the routing words and the table
   off the critical path, persistent blocks that walk several column tiles. The same applies to 16 streams (0.92x), whose steps are
   now on the native GEMM too.
2. **Full-tile energy** (gpt-oss serving prompt waves, prefill MoE): 64.7. Fewer `ldmatrix` bytes per MMA (A reused across two
   column halves of a 256-row tile pair), cheaper decode (the doubled-code construction in one `LOP3` + shift), wider column tiles.
3. **Qwen3 decode below 32 rows and q / k / v** (unchanged from §63.7 item 3).
4. **Attention at 128K** (both models ~0.93x; §63.7 item 4).

BB=bench/BatchBench/bin/Release/net11.0/BatchBench
BEFORE="SHARPLIGHT_NATIVE_MOE_MIN_ROWS=12"   # develop's hand-over from the skinny expert GEMM
$BB ~/models/hf/gpt-oss-20b --provider cuda --slots 64 --ctx 640 --depth 256 --sizes 1,16,32,48,64 --modes greedy --reps 20 --text

python bench/s54_vllm_decode_profile.py ~/models/hf/gpt-oss-20b --seqs 64 --words       # vLLM on the same word prompts
QUIET_GPU=1 ROUNDS=2 bench/s16_serve.sh sharplight gpt-oss-20b ~/models/hf/gpt-oss-20b "16 64" --provider cuda
cd bench/s56_moe && nvcc -O3 -arch=sm_120 -std=c++17 -DK=2880 -DN=2880 -DNFULL=5760 -DDUAL=1 -DNM_BM=32 -DNM_WM=1 -DNM_WN=8 -DNM_BN=128 \
  -DNM_STAGES=4 -DNM_MINB=2 -DKFILE='"../../src/Sharplight.Shaders/Kernels/gemm_moe_native.cu"' bench_moe.cu -o b && ./b

output in [`bench/results/s65/`](../bench/results/s65).

### 65.2 The expert GEMMs at decode sizes are at the read limit; what is left is split experts

§64.9 put the native grouped MXFP4 GEMM's decode tiles at ~650-670 GB/s against 730-790 for a plain `cp.async` ring over the same layout
(`read_pattern.cu`). Taken apart in the harness (`bench/s56_moe`, gate / up dual 32-row tiles, 4 stages, two blocks per SM, uniform
routing, T = 32 tokens, ms; `harness/ablation.txt`):

| variant | memset eviction (§56-64) | read eviction (`EVICT=read`, new) |
|---|---:|---:|
| the kernel (`develop`) | 0.406-0.408 | **0.358-0.360** (788 GB/s of weights and scales) |
| copies only (no decode, no MMAs) | 0.395-0.397 | |
| copies only, no scale copies | 0.379 | |
| copies only, no activation / scale copies, no routing reads, no factor table | 0.377 | |
| ... and no epilogue (no stores) | 0.352 | |
| the kernel without its stores | 0.377-0.379 | (no eviction at all: 0.356, the kernel 0.360) |
| `read_pattern.cu` (code bytes only), 1-5 blocks per SM | 0.346-0.360 | |

* The harness evicted the L2 before each launch with a 256 MB `cudaMemsetAsync`, which leaves it full of dirty lines that the
  kernel's reads then have to write back. Every variant pays for that, the ones with stores the most (the stores are only 1.5 MB, but
  they mix writes into the write-back stream). Evicted by a read of the same 256 MB (`EVICT=read`, closer to a decode step, where
  the preceding kernels read weights), the unchanged kernel reads 788 GB/s at 32-64 tokens (gate / up) and 767 GB/s (down, 0.184 ms),
  the read limit. So "650 GB/s" was a property of the harness, not of the kernel's copy issue. `read_pattern.cu` with an occupancy
  cap reads 762-767 GB/s from one block per SM up (`harness/read_pattern.txt`), so neither occupancy nor the number of resident blocks limits it.
* Rejected on the way (harness, memset eviction unless noted): **persistent blocks** that walk (routing tile, column tile) units with
  one copy ring across unit boundaries (the fill and drain of each block's 45-step ring were the suspect): decode tiles +2-4 % at
  2 blocks per SM, +15 % at 3, the 128-row tiles +7-14 % (more registers: 79 → 112 / 255 with spills) (`rejected/persistent_h1.txt`);
  the tile rows' item indices read into shared memory at the start instead of after the K loop: equal; **L1 prefetches of the
  epilogue's bias rows** at the start (`BIAS=1`, gpt-oss's per-expert biases, new in the harness: they cost ~1 %): equal; 64- and
  128-row column tiles for the down product (192 stays best).
* What does cost: **an expert split over two routing tiles**. Every 32-row tile reads its expert's weights again, and the second read
  costs ~62 % of a DRAM read even when the two tiles run at the same time (`SPLIT=1`: every expert's items over two tiles, gate / up
  0.360 → 0.580 ms, down 0.186 → 0.289; the launch order, column-tile or routing-tile major, makes no difference). In the harness with
  skewed routing (`SKEW=0.6`) a 64-token step takes 0.356 + 0.180 ms for both products, as the engine's 352 + 187 µs on text routing
  (§64.9's profile), and Marlin's ~471 µs is what reading the ~28 touched experts once costs at the read limit. The difference to
  vLLM in the decode step's expert GEMMs is therefore the experts that text routing gives 33-64 items, which the 32-row tiles split.
* **64-row decode tiles** (one tile per expert up to 64 items) need the 64-row tile at four stages, which fits two blocks per SM only
  without the 1 KB E8M0 factor table (`NM_TABLE=0`, factors converted at each decode: 2 x 51,200 bytes = the SM's 100 KB). In the
  harness, skewed routing: equal at 64 tokens (0.358 against 0.356 ms), -4 to -9 % at 128-256; uniform: +2.5-6 %. In the engine
  slower at every size (`--text`, GPU ms, 16 / 32 / 48 / 64 / 96 sequences: 12.72 / 16.02 / 17.89 / 19.32 / 22.57 with 32-row tiles,
  13.22 / 16.69 / 18.77 / 19.96 / 23.34 with 64-row tiles; `rejected/decode_rows64_engine.txt`), as §64's 64-row trial. Rejected.
* What this round keeps of it: the **short dual tiles (64 rows, 12-24 items per expert) take the table-free four-stage form**
  (`NM_TABLE=0` where four stages fit two blocks per SM only without the table, `NativeMoeConfig`; `SHARPLIGHT_NATIVE_MOE_TABLE=1` keeps
  the table and three stages). Harness, read eviction, 32-256 tokens: 0.381-0.463 → 0.369-0.457 ms (`harness/tiles64.txt`); gpt-oss-20b
  mixed steps (BatchBench `--mixed`, two alternated pairs, GPU ms): 64 + 107 rows 23.36 / 23.33 → 23.21 / 23.07, 64 + 150 rows 26.52 /
  26.63 → 26.49 / 26.61 (`engine/e2_*`). The factors are those of the table, so outputs are bit-identical. The harness has the read
  eviction (`EVICT=read`) and gpt-oss's bias epilogue (`BIAS=1`) as options now.

### 65.3 Prefill attention: two query fragments per warp at head size 64

At 128K, attention is 63 % of gpt-oss-20b's prefill (§64 profile: 13.85 of 22.0 s, ~122 TFLOPS over the 12 full-attention layers).
`attn_prefill_native.cu` had one 16-row query fragment per warp (`FN_MR=1`), so each K fragment loaded with `ldmatrix` fed two MMAs and
each V fragment two. With `FN_MR=2` (an option of the kernel since round 14, which §58 measured "the same" on a short prompt) every
fragment feeds four. It takes 255 registers (a 4-byte spill), so two blocks of 4 warps share an SM instead of three. In the harness
(`bench/s58_attn`, gpt-oss shapes: 64 query heads on 8 KV heads, head size 64, sinks, 2048 causal queries after n_past keys, best of 20,
ms; `attn_harness_d64.txt`):

| n_past | 0 | 14,336 | 30,720 | 63,488 | 126,976 | window 128 (any n_past) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 4 warps x 1 fragment (`develop`) | 0.254 | 3.54-3.55 | 7.49 | 15.83-15.91 | 31.49-31.57 (136 TFLOPS) | 0.102-0.106 |
| 8 warps x 1 | | | 8.01 | 16.34-16.37 | 32.36-32.41 | 0.115 |
| 4 warps x 1, three stages | | | 8.04 | 16.70-16.71 | 33.17-33.20 | |
| 2 warps x 2 | 0.264 | 3.73 | | 16.37-16.38 | | 0.100-0.104 |
| 8 warps x 2 | 0.256 | 3.45 | | 14.59-14.61 | | 0.115 |
| **4 warps x 2 (this round)** | **0.248** | **3.29-3.31** | **6.91** | **14.12-14.19** | **28.04-28.08 (153 TFLOPS)** | 0.102-0.106 |

The per-row arithmetic is unchanged (the same key tiles in the same order; a tile only the warp's other fragment sees adds exact zeros
with a correction factor of exactly 1), so outputs are bit-identical (65.6). The lowering takes two fragments at head size 64 and keeps
one at 128 (`NativeAttentionFragments`; `SHARPLIGHT_ATTN_MR=n`). gpt-oss-20b prefill, CUDA, before / after in the same lock hold
(median of 5, tok/s; `long/prefill_mr_ab.txt`):

| gpt-oss-20b | 16K | 32K | 64K | 128K |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `FN_MR=1` | 13,606 | 11,584 | 8,767 | 5,920 |
| **`FN_MR=2`** | **13,722 (+0.9 %)** | **11,811 (+2.0 %)** | **9,242 (+5.4 %)** | **6,478 (+9.4 %)** |
| vLLM (§58.8) | 14,496 | 12,327 | 9,440 | 6,435 |
| ours / vLLM | 0.93 → **0.95** | 0.94 → **0.96** | 0.93 → **0.98** | 0.92 → **1.01** |

The CUDA profile of the 128K prefill (`long/profile_gpt-oss-20b_131072.categories.txt`) has attention at 12.07 s of 20.25 s (§64: 13.85
of 22.04 s), 59.6 % of the prefill; the MoE (5.96 s) and the dense GEMMs (1.55 s) are unchanged. At 16K-32K, where attention is a
smaller share, the gap that is left (0.95-0.96x) is mostly the MoE glue and full tiles (§64.7).

### 65.4 Decode at depth: twice the split-KV workgroups on CUDA

A gpt-oss-20b decode step at 128K keys (1 stream, 10.0 ms GPU; `long/decode_128k_profile.txt`) spends 4.82 ms in `decode` attention:
0.39 ms per full-attention layer for its 268 MB of K / V, ~683 GB/s, 87 % of the read limit. The weights' matvecs are at the limit
(LM head 1.40 ms, 824 GB/s; the routed experts' int-dot matvec 45 µs for 35 MB). On PTX the split count aimed for 512 workgroups
(§58: so that 64 sequences at 256-token contexts run one key range per row without the combine), which gives a 128K row 64 ranges
of 2,048 keys per KV head, 512 workgroups of 128 threads: six per SM, half the occupancy the kernel allows. Sweep at 128K
(`SHARPLIGHT_ATTN_DECODE_CFG=workgroups,min keys,max ranges`, GPU ms per step, 1 / 4 streams; `long/decode_cfg_sweep_128k.txt`):

| configuration | 1 stream | 4 streams |
|---|---:|---:|
| 512 / 128 / 64 (PTX default before) | 9.99 | 25.52-25.60 |
| 1024 / 128 / 128 | 9.43 | 24.65 |
| 2048 / 128 / 256 | 9.56 | 24.39 |
| **1024 / 256 / 128 (this round's PTX default)** | **9.42** | **24.69** |

The 256-key minimum per range keeps short batched contexts on one range per row (64 sequences at 256 keys: 1024 / (64 x 8) = 2 ranges
asked for, 256 keys each, so one), as the 512-workgroup target did. Before / after at other shapes (alternated, GPU ms;
`engine/e6_*`):

| shape | gpt-oss-20b (head size 64) before → after | Qwen3-8B-FP8 (head size 128) with the same configuration |
|---|---|---|
| 1 / 16 / 32 / 64 sequences at 256 keys (`--text`) | 5.34 / 12.87-12.93 / 16.67-16.68 / 19.49-19.67 → 5.38 / 12.86 / 16.61-16.63 / 19.69-19.73 | 11.32 / 13.50-13.54 / 14.62-14.69 / 16.43-16.45 → 11.59 / 13.55 / 14.61-14.62 / 16.68-16.71 |
| 1 / 16 sequences at 3,500 keys | 5.46 / 12.25-12.32 → 5.42-5.44 / 12.19-12.22 | 11.77 / 23.18-23.21 → 11.82 / 23.62 |
| 1 / 4 streams at 32K keys | 6.37 / 11.88 → 6.39 / 11.66 | 17.13 / 36.04 → 17.26 / 37.61 |

At head size 128 the configuration costs 0.3-4.4 % everywhere, also where the range counts do not change (64 sequences at 256 keys:
one range either way), which points at the decode kernel's fused combine, whose per-split arrays grow with `DEC_MAX_SPLITS`; so the
PTX default is 1024 / 256 / 128 up to head size 64 and stays 512 / 128 / 64 above (`DecodeConfig`). For gpt-oss the short contexts
lose ~0.5 % (one sequence at 256 keys now runs one range of 256 instead of two of 128), the long ones gain 2-6 %.
