### 65.7 Gap to vLLM and plan (state after this round)

| benchmark | CUDA / vLLM | where the time goes |
|---|---:|---|
| gpt-oss-20b decode step, 64 sequences, generated tokens (`--feedback` / `--text`) | 0.88 / 0.87 (18.5 / 19.7 against 16.3 / 17.2 ms) | expert GEMMs ~12 ms at the read limit per tile; split experts (33-64 items on 32-row tiles) read twice |
| Qwen3-8B-FP8 decode step, 64 sequences (`--text` = `--feedback` = fixed ids: dense) | 0.94 (16.64 against 15.6 ms) | unchanged (§63.7) |
| gpt-oss-20b serving 16 / 64 streams | 0.93 / 0.86 | prompt waves on full tiles (power-limited, §64.7), decode steps as above |
| Qwen3-8B-FP8 serving 16 / 64 streams | 0.89 / 0.91 (§64) | its decode step; at 16 the generated fp8 GEMM below 32 rows |
| gpt-oss-20b long prefill 16K / 32K / 64K / 128K | 0.95 / 0.96 / 0.98 / 1.01 | MoE (52 % at 32K) and the 16K-32K attention |
| Qwen3-8B-FP8 long prefill (§63) | 0.97 / 0.98 / 1.01 / 0.94 | attention at head size 128 (one fragment per warp: two spill, Q in shared memory is slower, 65.3) |
| gpt-oss-20b decode at depth 32K / 128K, 1 / 4 streams | 1.04 / 1.10, 0.99 / 0.93 | decode attention at ~87 % of the read limit (1 stream) |

Ranked levers:

1. **Split experts in the decode step** (gpt-oss decode 0.87-0.88x, serving at 64 streams). Each block's speed is bound by its own copy
   latency, so a second 32-row tile over the same expert costs ~62 % of a fresh read (65.2) and the engine's expert GEMMs sit ~14 %
   above Marlin's read-once time. Uniform 64-row decode tiles lose in the engine; the candidate is a per-expert tile class in
   `moe_route`: 32-row tiles for experts with up to 32 items, one 64-row tile (a second launch of the four-stage table-free tile)
   for experts with 33-64, so every expert is read once. Estimated 0.3-0.9 ms per 64-sequence step (needs the engine's split count
   per layer, not measured: a routing histogram from `moe_route`'s scratch would give it).
2. **Head size 128 prefill attention** (Qwen3 128K 0.94x): two query fragments per warp need ~64 fewer live registers. Q in shared memory
   freed them but costs the extra `ldmatrix` traffic (130 against 141 TFLOPS); 32-key tiles (halving the score registers) or
   three-quarter fragments are the next candidates.
3. **Decode attention at depth**: the split count follows rows, not context length; a rule on the key count (more ranges per row
   only above ~16K keys) would keep the short-context steps on develop's launches (the 1024 / 256 / 128 configuration costs ~0.5 %
   at 64 sequences x 256 keys and 1 sequence, 65.4) and could take more ranges at 128K. At 1 stream the kernel is at ~87 % of the
   read limit.
4. **Qwen3 decode below 32 rows and q / k / v** (unchanged from §63.7 item 3): a multi-output form of the FP8 decode GEMM over q / k / v
   (k and v alone run at ~300 GB/s), and a decode form whose K split fills the GPU at 16-31 rows.
5. **Full-tile energy** (gpt-oss prompt waves, §64.9 item 2).

BEFORE="SHARPLIGHT_ATTN_MR=1 SHARPLIGHT_NATIVE_MOE_TABLE=1"   # develop's prefill attention and short expert tiles

## 66. MoE with CPU offload, round 3: split decode for gpt-oss, streamed layers in the stored layout, CPU kernels (exp, slot sum, K-quant dots), Qwen3-Coder-Next (2026-11-21)

Branch `perf/offload-r3` (base `develop` at `72962704`, §62 merged; `develop` merged again at `9ceeaeea`, StreamedExperts / Moe, a 122B CUDA bench and its FamilyGenerationTests rerun after the merge). Same machine and methodology as §59 / §62: GPU 0 of the RunPod machine
(RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell 32 GB, no resizable BAR), AMD EPYC 7443 with a 10.2-CPU cgroup quota shared by all jobs on the pod (AVX2, no
AVX-512) and a 62 GB cgroup memory limit, llama.cpp b11177; the GPU shared with another perf agent (runs serialized with a lock), the CPU with
a model-feed job. Sharplight: `sharplight <model> --provider cuda|vulkan --cpu-offload --bench 512` (prefill best of 5 warm 512-token passes,
and their median; decode 64 steps, best / median tok/s); llama.cpp: `llama-bench -ngl 99 -ncmoe N -fa 1 -p 512 -n 64 -r 3 -t 10` (mean ± sd
of 3), N swept, the best shown. gpt-oss-120b decode varies by ±15 % between identical runs (its 20 CPU expert layers read 33 GB per token
range; the cgroup throttled 14 % of all periods during this round), so its rows give two runs.

### 66.1 Results against llama.cpp (tok/s)

| model, provider | decode before (§62) | decode now (2 runs) | llama.cpp decode | prefill before | prefill now (best / median) | llama.cpp prefill |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Qwen3.5-122B-A10B UD-IQ2_XXS, CUDA | 72.2 / 69.9 | **74.5 / 70.1**, 73.3 / 70.4 | 71.0 ± 0.3 (`-ncmoe 6`) | 999 | **998** / 997 | 966 ± 59 |
| Qwen3.5-122B-A10B UD-IQ2_XXS, Vulkan | 67.2 / 60.2, 71.1 / 66.3 | 63.6 / 56.7, 62.4 / 54.9 | 45.9 ± 0.5 | 1071 / 1003 | 1031 / 1023, 960 / 874 | 745 ± 9 |
| gpt-oss-120b MXFP4, CUDA | 49.3 / 42.9 | **51.7 / 46.0**, 53.0 / 44.9 (54.1 / 51.3 earlier) | 36.4 ± 6.4 (`-ncmoe 20`) | 283 / 278 | **305** / 300, 289 / 282 | 109 ± 65 |
| gpt-oss-120b MXFP4, Vulkan | 50.7 / 49.1 | **50.3 / 48.9**, 51.1 / 49.7 | 33.6 ± 3.5 (`-ncmoe 22`) | 112 / 78 | **311** / 305, 307 / 304 | 110 ± 32 |
| Qwen3-Coder-Next Q4_K_M (new), CUDA | | 74.2 / 70.1, 74.9 / 67.1 | **97.0 ± 3.7** (`-ncmoe 16`) | | 665 / 664 | 597 ± 18 |
| Qwen3-Coder-Next Q4_K_M (new), Vulkan | | **76.9 / 74.5**, 76.6 / 74.0 | 55.2 ± 1.7 (`-ncmoe 20`) | | **543** / 531 | 385 ± 4 |

* Against llama.cpp's best setting: Qwen3.5-122B CUDA decode 1.03-1.05x (best; medians 0.99x), prefill 1.03x; Vulkan decode 1.36-1.39x,
  prefill 1.29-1.38x. gpt-oss-120b CUDA decode 1.42-1.46x, prefill 2.7x; Vulkan decode 1.50-1.52x, prefill 2.8x. Qwen3-Coder-Next Vulkan
  decode 1.39x, prefill 1.41x; **CUDA decode 0.77x** (prefill 1.11x), the one result below the target (66.4).
* llama.cpp's gpt-oss-120b numbers are lower and noisier than §59's (36.4 against 40.4 decode on CUDA, prefill ± 60 %): its 20-22 CPU expert
  layers read from a page cache that the 63 GB file overflows; `-ncmoe 24` on Vulkan (15.7) left too little memory for the cache.
* The 122B Vulkan decode medians are below §62's (55-57 against 60-66); the same build without host imports (`host_memory_import`
  disabled, 67.2 / 64.6, 1065 prefill, 66.3) and these runs came at different load, and the 122B CUDA runs of the same hour matched §62.

### 66.2 Changes

* **Split decode for experts with per-expert tables** (gpt-oss): sparse compilations keep the stored weight layout (no MXFP4 repack: they copy
  single experts from the mapped file), and the per-expert tables the segment gathers by the same ids (`GatherAxis`, the experts' biases) are
  held whole on the GPU, their rows copied into the slot rows with the banks; the rows past the slots stay zero, so the ids of -1 read zeros.
  On the CPU a slot of -1 still adds its bias, so a layer whose ids feed such gathers qualifies only with one input of slot weights that
  scales the slots right before the slot sum; a split pass zeroes the other side's weights. Layers whose banks are not page-locked are not
  split (their copies would take the host thread). `SparseExpertLayout` / `SparseExpertSelection` are shared by CUDA and Vulkan.
* **The split share by measured pass time** (`SplitBalance`): per layer and row count, the smoothed time of whole passes per GPU share from 0
  (the CPU alone) to all slots, the fastest taken, an unmeasured neighbor tried at once and a measured one every 8 passes, the first pass of a
  share discarded as warm-up. For gpt-oss a GPU slot (13 MB over the bus, ~0.47 ms) costs about twice a CPU slot, so the shares settle at 1-2 of
  4 (split layers 0.89-0.98 ms against 1.0-1.1 ms on the CPU alone); the old rule (one slot up or down by the wait) oscillated and could not
  choose the CPU alone.
* **Streamed layers in the stored layout**: streamed compilations no longer repack MXFP4 / Q8_0 / FP8 experts, so their copies go straight
  from the page-locked (CUDA) pages instead of being repacked on the host into staging: gpt-oss-120b prefill CUDA 264 → 315 and Vulkan
  145 → 239 tok/s in the A/B runs (Vulkan stages unrepacked rows at ~17 GB/s against ~5-10 GB/s with the repack), 300-311 in the final runs.
* **Page-lock budget**: mapped weights may be page-locked (CUDA) or imported (Vulkan) up to half of the process memory (was a quarter): the
  CPU's expert pages, which every decode step reads, then stay in memory. gpt-oss-120b: 13 of 20 CPU layers locked (all 20 with
  `SHARPLIGHT_LIMIT_PINNED_HOST_MEMORY=40G`: decode 54.8 / 52.5 and 46.3 / 42.9 in two runs, prefill 374 with the stored layout).
* **CPU exp**: `Vector256.Exp` of the runtime ran scalar, ~27 ns per value (SiLU of 8192 values 228 µs). `VectorExp` (Cephes `expf`, 2 ulp,
  flushes below e^-87.3) serves SiLU, sigmoid, softmax, attention and the float lanes: 5.8 µs. In the 122B's CPU expert layers SiLU was
  0.09-0.12 ms of ~0.55; other unary kernels are still slow (tanh 100 µs, softplus 83 µs, erf 24 µs, mish 258 µs per 8192 values).
* **Slot sum in place** (`AxisSumOp`): `ReduceSum(Permute(x, 0, 2, 1))` over a [T, k, H] tensor adds the k rows of H values instead of
  materializing the permuted view and reducing rows of k (Copy 28 µs + ReduceSum 32 µs → 4 µs per 122B layer).
* **Fused Q4_K and Q6_K integer dots** (AVX2): the 4- and 6-bit codes times the 8-bit activations per 32 values (`vpmaddubsw`), scaled per
  sub-block in float, the mins / offset from the activation row's group sums; no decoded row is written. Q4_K 2.50 against 3.99 ns per 32
  values (decode + dot). They serve `MatMulId` and `MatMul` (every Q4_K / Q6_K product on the CPU). Qwen3-Coder-Next CUDA decode 69.6 → 74-75.
* **Vulkan host-memory imports** (VK_EXT_external_memory_host, feature `host_memory_import`, the page-lock budget): streamed and selected
  experts are copied from imported pages on the device queue, which enables the split decode on Vulkan (`StreamsSelectedExperts`). The device
  probes one import when it opens and leaves the imports off when the driver refuses. On this machine the NVIDIA driver refuses every import,
  even 64 KiB of anonymous memory (`ErrorOutOfDeviceMemory`): it pins through the locked-memory limit, 8 MiB in this container without
  `CAP_IPC_LOCK`, while `cuMemHostRegister` is not bound by it. Before the probe, the failed imports cost device memory (three
  out-of-memory re-placements and an unstreamed layer: 122B Vulkan prefill 496-779 against 1065). The Vulkan split is therefore not
  exercised on this machine (the `StreamedExpertsTests` split cases run without sparse compilations on Vulkan).

### 66.3 What did not work

* **Waking the CPU workers before a CPU segment** (they spin 1 ms from the start of the GPU segment before it): mean decode 49.8 against 67.9
  without (median 69.6 / 70.1), from cgroup throttling: nine spinning workers use up the pod's shared 10-CPU quota. Reverted.
* **MXFP4 dot with two accumulators** (1.64 against 1.61 ns per 32 values) and with a variable shift instead of the 128-bit insert
  (2.15 ns): the loop is not bound by its FMA chain. Not kept.
* **All 20 gpt-oss layers split** (40 GB lock budget, old balancer): 1.1 ms per layer against 0.95 on the CPU alone; the copies (21 MB per
  layer per token) also take memory bandwidth from the CPU's share.
* Qwen3-Coder-Next on CUDA: 17 split layers (512 experts of 1.8 MB, top 10) at 0.43-0.56 ms plus 0.12-0.17 ms of attention segment each, and
  5.4 ms of GPU time; llama.cpp's whole step is 10.3 ms. The split barely helps (69.9 against 69.2 without in the profile runs) and Vulkan
  without it is faster (76.9); next: the CPU expert products at this shape (31-33 GB/s before the fused dots), fewer launches per layer.

plus our 1.6 ms LM head and sampling, §64). Raw output in [`bench/results/s67/`](../bench/results/s67).

### 67.2 Real-text routing: few split experts, and the tile class is worth at most 0.26 ms

§65.7's first lever was a per-expert tile class (experts with 33-64 items on one 64-row tile instead of two 32-row tiles). A routing
histogram of BatchBench `--text` decode steps (the 32-row tiles of every gate / up launch, 9 steps x 24 layers per batch size; a temporary
print in the kernel, `harness/routing_histogram_text.txt`):

| sequences (items) | experts touched per layer | experts with 17-32 / 33-48 / 49-64 items | split experts per layer (> 32 items) | > 64 items |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|
| 16 (64) | 17.9 | 0 / 0 / 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 32 (128) | 23.8 | 1.23 / 0 / 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 48 (192) | 27.0 | 2.50 / 0.48 / 0 | 0.48 | 0 |
| 64 (256) | 27.2 | 3.38 / 0.80 / 0.31 | 1.11 | 0 |

The 216 per-layer routings of the 64-sequence steps replayed in the harness (`bench/s56_moe`, new `ROUTES=file`: each routing one launch,
read eviction, best of 10, ms per layer; `harness/tile_class_routes.txt`):

| product | 32-row tiles (`develop`) | 64-row routing: <= 32 items on 32-row tiles + 33-64 on a second, 64-row launch | read-once bound (`CLAMP=1`: split tiles cut to 32 rows) | uniform 64-row tiles |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| gate / up (dual) | 0.309 | 0.279 + 0.043 = 0.322 | 0.300 | 0.313 |
| down | 0.164 | 0.148 + 0.040 = 0.188 | 0.162 | 0.174 |

Reading every expert once would save 11 µs per layer (0.26 ms per step, 1.4 %); a second launch for the 33-64-item class loses (its
handful of blocks runs alone), so the class would have to live in one launch with both tile heights. §65's "62 % of a fresh read" holds
when every expert is split (`SPLIT=1`); on text routing one expert in 27 is. Not built; it moves down the plan.

The same replay also shows that the harness's 0.473 ms per layer for both products equals vLLM's Marlin in its own step (11.36 ms for 48
launches, §64), while the engine's profile has ~0.53 ms. The difference is the clock: back to back over the 216 routings and 24 distinct
weight copies (`LAYERS=24`, new; distinct copies make no difference to the same copy, so page-table reach is not it), gate / up takes
0.365-0.372 ms per layer against 0.326 isolated, at the 200 W limit with the SM clock at ~1.78 GHz instead of 2.5-2.6 GHz
(`harness/clocks_gate_up_sustained.txt`); down 0.181 against 0.172 (~1.86 GHz). So in a decode step the expert GEMMs are energy-bound,
and the instructions per weight byte are what is left to cut.

### 67.3 The E2M1 decode in fewer instructions

The decode of the MXFP4 codes is most of the K loop's instructions (per 8 weights: a 16-byte shared load, five byte permutes, ~20 masks,
shifts and ors, eight f16 multiplications; the MMAs and copies are a fraction). Two changes, both giving the same halves bit for bit:

* Each code pair was masked into the low bits of a word and then shifted into the half layout of `fp4_h2` (magnitude at bits 9..11, sign at
  15). Now two byte permutes put the four code bytes into bytes 1 and 3 of two words, so each half holds its byte in bits 8..15, and each
  pair is one shift and one three-input logic operation (`nm_e2m1_hi` / `nm_e2m1_lo`), as Marlin's FP4 dequantization does.
* The second scale factor `s2` (the E8M0 factor split in two halves for the range of f16) is exactly 1.0 for every E8M0 byte up to 127,
  i.e. every factor up to 1 (all of gpt-oss's); it is now multiplied only above, behind a branch that is uniform where a block's scales are.

Sustained replay (216 routings over 24 weight copies, ms per layer, three alternated passes; `harness/decode_variants_sustained.txt`):

| gate / up variant | sustained | isolated |
|---|---:|---:|
| `develop` | 0.365-0.372 | 0.326-0.328 |
| shared loads of the two used words instead of 16 bytes (`lds32`) | 0.368-0.369 | 0.326-0.327 |
| without the `s2` multiplication | 0.357-0.363 | 0.324-0.325 |
| **new decode, `s2` above 127 only (this round)** | **0.355-0.357** | 0.323-0.324 |
| down: `develop` → this round | 0.181 → 0.177 | 0.172 → 0.170 |

What is left: without any MMAs the sustained gate / up takes 0.327 ms, without the decode 0.342, without both 0.318 against 0.348-0.352
for the kernel (`harness/diag_and_attn128.txt`): the copies and the memory read are ~90 % of it now. The harness checks the products against
its reference also with E8M0 bytes 126-133 (`-DSCALE_BASE=126`, new: the `s2` path), and its reference decode no longer uses the kernel's.

### 67.4 A multi-output form of the FP8 decode GEMM (q / k / v)

Qwen3-8B-FP8's q / k / v [4096 → 4096 + 1024 + 1024] ran the K-split multi-output GEMM (40.6 + 2.8 µs per layer at 64 rows, §63.3); on the
hand-written decode form each matrix alone ran 24.4 + 2 x 13.7 µs (k and v: 16 blocks, ~300 GB/s). `gemm_fp8_native.cu` takes `MULTI`
(2 or 3 members, `MULTI_O1` / `MULTI_O2`): each 64-row weight tile lies in one member's matrix (the boundaries are multiples of 128) and
stores to that member's output, one launch over the 96 tiles; each output sums its K blocks as its own decode-form launch would.
Decode steps (`--text`, GPU ms, two alternated pairs; `decode/qwen_*`): 64 sequences 16.65 → 16.48, 48: 15.58-15.59 → 15.45-15.48, but
32: 14.66-14.67 → 14.92-14.98. The launch takes 42.0 µs (min) at 64 rows: 96 blocks at one per SM run two waves, so it saves the reduction
and not much of the read. It serves 48-64 rows (`NativeFp8MultiMinRows`); final build in 67.1. `CudaCodeTests.NativeFp8MultiGemmMatchesTheCpu`
(48 and 64 rows, 512 + 128 + 128 outputs, against the CPU and the generated fp8 GEMM).

### 67.5 What did not work

* **32-key tiles for two query fragments per warp at head size 128** (§65.7 item 2; `FN_BC=32`, which halves the score registers):
  Qwen3 shapes in `bench/s58_attn` (32 query heads on 8 KV heads, 2048 causal queries, ms; `harness/diag_and_attn128.txt`):

  | n_past | 0 | 30,720 | 126,976 |
  |---|---:|---:|---:|
  | 8 warps x 1 fragment, 64 keys, 3 stages (`develop`) | **0.268** | **7.67** | **30.8 (139 TFLOPS)** |
  | 4 x 2, 32 keys, 3 stages | 0.279 | 7.93 | 31.9 |
  | 8 x 2, 32 keys, 3 stages | 0.291 | 8.72 | 35.1 |
  | 4 x 2, 32 keys, 4 stages | 0.342 | 9.81 | 39.4 |
  | 8 x 1, 32 keys, 4 stages | 0.283 | 8.34 | 33.5 |

  Two fragments still take 255 registers with 32-key tiles (68-byte spill), and the halved tiles double the block barriers and softmax
  rescales per key. Withdrawn.
* **Sharing the gate / up routing with the down product**: the profile shows two `moe_route` launches per expert block (960 per 20
  steps). Giving both products' grouped-launch conditions the same delegate (the routing cache compares them by reference) did not change
  the count, so another key of the cache differs; reverted (~3 µs x 24 per step, not found this round).
* The tile class of 67.2 as a second launch (loses), uniform 64-row decode tiles (lose, as §65).

### 67.7 Gap to vLLM and plan (state after this round)

| benchmark | CUDA / vLLM | where the time goes |
|---|---:|---|
| gpt-oss-20b decode step, 64 sequences (`--text` / `--feedback`) | 0.88 / 0.88 (19.5 / 18.4 against 17.2 / 16.3 ms) | expert GEMMs ~12.5 ms, energy-bound at the power limit (copies and reads ~90 % of them now); dense projections with split-K reductions; ~20 small launches per layer |
| Qwen3-8B-FP8 decode step, 64 sequences | 0.95 (16.49 against 15.6 ms) | q / k / v 42 µs per layer (two block waves), gate / up / down at 92-96 % of the read limit |
| gpt-oss-20b serving 16 / 64 streams | 0.93 / 0.88 | prompt waves on full expert tiles (power-limited), decode steps as above |
| Qwen3-8B-FP8 serving 16 / 64 streams | 0.89 / 0.92 | 16 streams: the generated fp8 GEMMs below 32 rows |
| Qwen3-8B-FP8 long prefill 128K | 0.94 | attention at head size 128 (one fragment per warp) |
| gpt-oss-20b long prefill 16K / 32K / 64K / 128K | 0.96 / 0.97 / 0.99 / 1.00 | MoE and attention at 16K-32K |
| gpt-oss-20b decode at depth 32K / 128K, 1 / 4 streams | 1.04 / 1.11, 0.99 / 0.93 | decode attention at ~87 % of the read limit |

Ranked levers:

1. **gpt-oss dense projections at decode sizes**: q / k / v [2880 → 5120] and o [4096 → 2880] run the split-K gemm_cm2 plus a reduction
   (and o a ranged-f16 conversion), ~89 µs per layer in the profile against vLLM's ~74 µs of CUTLASS tiles. A decode form of
   `gemm_f16_native.cu` (64-row token and weight tiles, no K split, as the FP8 decode form of §63.3) and the q / k / v multi-output form of
   67.4 on it: estimated 0.3-0.4 ms per 64-sequence step.
2. **Fewer small launches in the gpt-oss step** (~20 per layer of 2-7 µs: two routings per expert block, two gathers, the router's
   to_f16 + split-K + reduce, topk, softmax, rope, norms): find why the down product re-routes (67.5: not the launch condition), fuse the
   router GEMM's chain. ~0.1-0.3 ms.
3. **Qwen3 decode below 32 rows** (serving at 16 streams): a decode form of the FP8 GEMM whose K split fills the GPU at 16-31 rows, and
   q / k / v at 32-47 rows (the multi-output form lost there: two waves of 96 blocks; 32-row weight tiles or a K split of 2).
4. **Per-expert tile class in one launch** (67.2): at most 0.26 ms per 64-sequence step on text routing (1.4 %), both tile heights in one
   kernel (template on the tile rows, smem of the larger).
5. **Expert GEMM copies**: each 32-row decode tile copies its expert's activation rows once per column block (45 blocks per expert for
   gate / up); with the decode now cheaper, the copies and their L2 traffic are what the power limit pays for. Wider column tiles per
   block with two weight tiles in flight, or a cluster-shared activation tile (distributed shared memory, sm_90+).
6. **Head size 128 prefill attention** (Qwen3 128K 0.94x): 32-key tiles lose (67.5); left: two fragments with the output accumulators
   split over two warps along DV, or the Q fragments of the second fragment re-read from shared memory.
7. **Decode attention split by key count** (~0.5 % at short contexts, ~1 % at 128K x 4 streams, §65.4).

### 68.2 A decode form of the hand-written f16 GEMM (gpt-oss q / k / v and o)

gpt-oss-20b's attention projections are bf16 (stored as f16 for the library path). At 33-256 rows they ran gemm_cm2 with a K split
and a reduction: q / k / v [2880 → 4096 + 512 + 512] as the split-K multi-output GEMM (41.9 + 4.4 µs min per layer at 64 rows) and o
[4096 → 2880] as gemm_cm2 split-K (38.0) + reduction (3.4) on a row-ranged f16 copy (3.1). `gemm_f16_native.cu` has a third tile
configuration, `H_CFG` 2: 64 tokens x `H_DBN` weight rows (64, or 32 where 64-row tiles would leave a quarter of the SMs without a
block), 2 x (`H_DBN` / 16) warps of 32 x 16 outputs, four stages of 64-value K steps, no K split, with the bias store and the
row-range unscale of the existing forms, and a multi-output form (`MULTI`, `MULTI_O1`, `MULTI_O2`: each weight tile in one member's
matrix, stored to that member's output with its bias; the FP8 kernel's scheme of §67.4). The lowering emits it for the split-K batches
of 33-64 rows (`NativeF16DecodeMinRows`): inside `EmitSplitKMatMul` for single matmuls whose epilogue is none or a lone bias row, and
in the multi-output group for q / k / v.

Harness (`bench/s68_f16dec`, 64 rows, µs; "sustained": 24 distinct weight copies back to back; `harness/`):

| variant | q / k / v sustained | o sustained |
|---|---:|---:|
| 64-row weight tiles, four stages | **39.4** (80 blocks, 748 GB/s) | 33.3 (45 blocks) |
| 32-row weight tiles | 39.0-40.2 (160 blocks) | **32.0** (90 blocks, two per SM) |
| six stages | 39.0 | 32.6-40.3 |
| `cp.async` with `L2::128B` / `L2::256B` prefetch | 39.5 / 39.5 | 32.0 |

In the engine's 64-sequence profile (`decode/gptoss_profile_final.txt`): q / k / v 43.7 µs mean per layer (was 43.8 + 5.8 for the
split GEMM and its reduction), o 35.7 (was 42.7 + 5.3; its f16 copy stays, 4.2): 102 → 84 µs per layer with the copy, against vLLM's
~74. Starting at 17 rows instead loses (16 / 32 sequences 12.71 / 16.44 → 13.33 / 16.60 ms: at 32 rows the 64-row token tile is half
padding and the clamped rows re-read the same lines, 46 µs against 39 at 64 rows). `SHARPLIGHT_NATIVE_F16_DECODE_BN=0` turns it off,
`=32` / `=64` force the weight tile. `CudaCodeTests.NativeF16DecodeGemmMatchesTheCpu` (40 and 64 rows, one projection and q / k / v
with biases, K = 2880, against the CPU and the generated GEMM).

### 68.3 One routing per expert block; the router's top-k and softmax in one launch

* **The second `moe_route` per block** (§67.5): the routing cache is keyed by the launch condition's reference. gpt-oss's gate / up
  pair is lowered with no condition, but its down product goes through the expert-sum path, which first emits the int-dot expert
  matvec and lowers the grouped product under `outer && items > 8` (a new delegate). r19 shared the delegate between products, but the
  gate / up product never had one. A routing emitted for every batch now serves a later product of the same ids whatever its condition,
  provided the tiling matches: the cache key adds the route tile heights and the item bounds that choose them (`skinnyItems`,
  `wideItems`, `wideTile`, `nativeMinItems`). 960 → 480 routing launches per 20 steps (2.7 µs each), 511 → 487 dispatches per step.
* **TopK then Softmax** (gpt-oss: the softmax of the four selected logits): `FuseRouterTopK` fused only Softmax → TopK (Qwen3-MoE's
  order). The TopK unit now also absorbs a Softmax that alone reads its values, and `topk_softmax` (`SELECTED_SOFTMAX`) selects on the raw
  logits and computes the softmax of the K selected values with the lanes and sums of `rows.slang`'s softmax over the [rows, K] values,
  so the probabilities are bit-identical. One launch less per layer (535 → 511 dispatches per step; topk 1.8 + softmax 2.0 µs → 3.8-4.2 µs: launch overhead, not
  kernel time, is what it saves). Both changes apply on Vulkan too.

Together with 68.2: gpt-oss-20b 64-sequence step 19.51-19.55 → 19.05 ms (`--text`), 18.37-18.40 → 17.88-17.90 (`--feedback`); 583 →
487 dispatches per step.

### 68.4 32-row token tiles for the FP8 decode form, and the FP8 GEMM from 9 rows (Qwen3 below 32 rows)

At 16-31 rows Qwen3-8B-FP8 ran its projections on the skinny GEMM (f16 activations, 16 rows) or the generated fp8 GEMM with a K split
(17-31), and q / k / v as the skinny q plus split-K k / v and two reductions (57.6 µs mean per layer at 16 rows, ~520 GB/s). The FP8
decode form (64 x 64 tiles, four stages, 66 KB: one block per SM) pads a 16- or 32-row batch to 64 rows. With `F8N_BM` 32 (already
supported by the kernel: three stages, 38 KB, two blocks per SM), `bench/s57_gemm` at 16 / 32 rows (µs, after an L2 flush;
`decode/fp8_tile_rows.txt`):

| shape | 64-row token tiles | 32-row token tiles |
|---|---:|---:|
| [4096 → 4096] | 41 / 35 | **29 / 29** |
| gate / up [4096 → 2 x 12288] | 170 / 162 | **141 / 143** |
| down [12288 → 4096] | 92 / 84 | **84 / 82** |

The decode form now takes 32-row token tiles up to 32 rows (`NativeFp8ShortTileMaxRows`), for single matmuls, dual gate / up and the
multi-output q / k / v (which before served only 48-64 rows: at 9-32 rows its 96 blocks fit at two per SM), and starts at 9 rows
(`NativeFp8DecodeMinRows`, was 32) together with the fp8 GEMM itself for the weights it takes (`Fp8GemmMinRows` per matmul: 9 for
`f8e4m3_b128g` weights with N a multiple of 128 where the decode form exists, else 17). Threshold sweep (GPU ms, `qwen/`): decode form
from 17 rows: 24 sequences 14.15 → 13.44; plus the 32-row q / k / v: 13.17-13.18, 32: 13.77-13.78, 20: 13.98 → 12.97; FP8 GEMM from 9
rows: 12: 13.06-13.18 → 12.44-12.52, 16: 13.53-13.69 → 12.91-12.95, 8 unchanged. Final build in 68.1. In the 16-sequence profile
(`final/qwen_profile_16.txt`) q / k / v is 38.0 µs mean per layer (was 57.6), down 73.2 (75.4), o 27.3 (28.8); the dual gate / up stays
on the skinny GEMM at 16 rows (139.6 µs; the harness shows no gain for 32-row tiles there).

Below 17 rows the activations are now quantized to E4M3 as they were from 17 rows (vLLM quantizes FP8 activations at every batch size);
greedy text (one sequence) is unaffected. `NativeFp8MultiGemmMatchesTheCpu` gains 16 and 32 rows (against the CPU; against the generated
path only from 17 rows, which below runs the skinny GEMM on f16 activations).

### 68.5 What did not work

* L2 prefetch hints on the f16 decode form's copies and six stages instead of four (68.2 table): within 1 %, or slower for o; removed.
* The f16 decode form from 17 rows (68.2): loses at 16-32 sequences.
* The router GEMM [2880 → 32] (to_f16 2.4 + split-K 6.1 + reduction 1.8 µs per layer) has 32 outputs: the decode form's weight tiles
  would fill one or two SMs; not attempted (see the plan).
* The fused `topk_softmax` launch is not faster than `topk_subgroup` + `softmax` in kernel time (3.8-4.2 against 3.8 µs); it saves the
  launch only. On Vulkan the one-sequence step is 0.02 ms slower in both pairs (5.32 → 5.34 ms).

Ranked levers:

1. **Expert GEMM copy traffic** (§67.7 item 5; the expert GEMMs are 66 % of the gpt-oss step and energy-bound): each 32-row decode tile

   weight tiles in flight, or a cluster-shared activation tile (distributed shared memory).
2. **The router chain of gpt-oss** (~10 µs per layer at 64 rows: f16 copy, split-K GEMM [2880 → 32], reduction with the bias, then the
   fused top-k): one kernel per row block reading the f32 norm output, the 32 logits, top-4 and softmax in registers (0.2 ms per step;
   logits in another summation order, so greedy may move at near-ties), or the norm writing the router's f16 copy (0.05 ms, exact).
3. **The o projection's f16 copy** (to_f16_ranged, 4.2 µs per layer): the attention combine writes the row-ranged f16 rows (0.1 ms).
4. **Qwen3 dense FP8 at 64 rows** (gate / up 134.6 µs: 384 blocks of 64 x 32 outputs at one per SM, 4.7 waves): the 32-row token tile
   halves the shared memory per block; a 64 x 64-row tile in three stages (50 KB) would put two blocks per SM.
5. **Per-expert tile class in one launch** (§67.2): at most 0.26 ms per 64-sequence gpt-oss step.
6. **Head size 128 prefill attention** (Qwen3 128K 0.94x, §67.7 item 6).
7. **Decode attention split by key count** (§65.4).

and the benches below after that merge). Same machine and methodology as §66: GPU 0 of the RunPod machine (RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell 32 GB),
AMD EPYC 7443 with a 10.2-CPU cgroup quota shared by every job on the pod (AVX2), 62 GB cgroup, llama.cpp b11177; the GPU shared with

gpt-oss: §66's numbers).

### 69.2 Where the Coder-Next step went

At the start (§66, CUDA): 17 CPU expert layers (layers 0-16; layer 17 resident in the streaming memory, 30 on the GPU, as llama.cpp's
`-ncmoe 16` minus one) at 0.49-0.60 ms per split pass, 18 GPU segments of one layer's attention at 0.15 ms of host time each (0.09 ms on
the device), and 3.8 ms of device time for the 30 GPU layers: ~14 ms per step. In the CPU segments the Q4_K / Q6_K dots ran at 2.5 / 3.4 ns
per 32 values (about the throughput of the memory bus for ten threads, so the products ran at 25-30 GB/s with the threads waiting on each
other), SiLU took 30-45 µs for 5120 values, and every layer ran seven parallel ops. A GPU segment made 9 driver calls around its graph
launch (nsys: scalar upload, two forwarded inputs, two events, two downloads and a synchronous upload and download of the
[512, 2048]-sized values), ~60 µs of host time per layer. The split balance had settled on 5-6 GPU slots, slower than the CPU alone once
the CPU got faster (sweeps: 68-69 against 79-84 tok/s), since it only compared neighbouring shares.

Now (quiet minute, `SHARPLIGHT_SEGMENT_TIMING=1`): CPU expert layers 0.29-0.33 ms of per-op minima (gate / up 0.19 ms at 62 GB/s, the
down product with the slot sum 0.10-0.15 ms) and 0.37-0.47 ms mean per split pass; GPU segments 0.11-0.13 ms of host time (one graph
launch, 0.03 ms submit); 10.8-10.9 ms best step. A 20 MB read of random 1.8 MB chunks by 8-11 threads takes 0.21-0.27 ms on this machine
(a C probe), so the CPU passes are within ~1.4x of the bus.

### 69.3 Changes

* **Q4_K and Q6_K fused dots, llama.cpp's form** (AVX2): the code-activation pair sums are weighted by the 6-bit sub-block scales in int16
  lanes (`vpmaddwd`) instead of scaling every 32 values in float, the scales unpacked once per block, the mins / offset terms of a block in
  one vector: 1.30 / 1.51 against 2.51 / 3.36 ns per 32 values at K = 2048 (single thread, cache-resident). Two rows per call for rows of
  K <= 512 (the down products): 1.40 / 1.64 against 2.07 / 2.33 ns, the same result as one row bit for bit; at K = 2048 a pair spills
  registers and is not used.
* **The CPU expert MLP in two passes**: a gate / up `MatMulId` pair followed by `Mul(Silu(gate), up)` writes the gated activation in its
  integer-dot units (after the float path for prefill), and the down product followed by `ReduceSum(Permute(Mul(y, w), 0, 2, 1))` writes the
  weighted slot sum (a unit takes 32 output rows of one token over every slot; more rows sum after the products), the slot products
  added in slot order like the separate ops. Up to 16k activation values are quantized on the calling thread. Seven parallel ops per layer
  became two, with the same results as before (tests compare with the separate nodes bit for bit).
* **CUDA steps as one graph**: a segment's small inputs and outputs (up to 1 MiB) go through page-locked staging buffers; the downloads, the
  runtime scalar upload, the inputs forwarded from other segments and the timing events are captured in the step's graph (the uploads are
  queued on the segment's stream), so a GPU segment of a CPU-offloaded layer costs one `cuGraphLaunch` and one wait: 0.15 → 0.11-0.13 ms of
  host time per segment. A split pass's expert copies from page-locked memory go in one `cuMemcpyBatchAsync` (drivers from 13.0), host time
  before the CPU starts 0.05-0.07 → 0.025-0.045 ms.
* **Split balance**: every third probe tries the CPU alone (a share of one GPU slot pays the GPU's fixed costs, so a search over neighbours
  stayed at 5-6 slots); with the faster CPU it settles at 2-4 slots.
* **Unary kernels**: tanh (Cephes `tanhf`), softplus (`max(x, 0) + log1p(e^-|x|)`, log1p from Cephes `logf` with Goldberg's correction) and
  mish (`x n / (n + 2)`, n = e^x (e^x + 2)) on `VectorExp`, within 4 ulp of double precision. Inside one large switch the JIT ran out of
  inlining budget and called `VectorExp` out of line in the later cases; the vector loops now have methods of their own. Per 8192 values:
  SiLU 34 → 6.4 µs, tanh 100 → 7.6, softplus 83 → 15, mish 258 → 7.0, GELU 57 → 25, erf 24 (unchanged: its double-precision vector
  form meets the 2e-7 bound the tests set).
* Diagnostics: segment timing shows each GPU segment's device, submit and wait times and a split pass's host time before its CPU work;
  `BenchTests.ExpertLayerThroughput`, `FusedDotThroughput` and `UnaryKernelThroughput` (`SHARPLIGHT_BENCH=1`).

### 69.4 What did not work or was not done

* **The split for Coder-Next** is worth little: its GPU slots copy 1.8 MB experts over a 23 GB/s bus while the CPU, which shares the memory
  bandwidth with those copies, slows down by ~50 % per slot (0.075 against 0.05 ms). Fixed 5 slots: 73 tok/s against 79-84 for the CPU
  alone in the same hour; the balancer's best shares are now within noise of the CPU alone.
* **Thread count and spin** (`SHARPLIGHT_CPU_THREADS` 8 / 10 / 11, `SHARPLIGHT_CPU_SPIN_US` 0 / 50 / 200): 10 threads 86.6 / 82.1 and 8
  threads 81.6 / 76.4 against 82.9-89.6 / 77-79 at the default in the interleaved runs, not separable from the pod's load (spin 0 lost
  40 % of the mean to wake-ups); the default stays (11 threads = the rounded-up quota, 200 µs).
* **Prefetch distance** in the expert units (0-8 rows ahead): no difference above the noise.
* **One layer fewer on the CPU**: llama.cpp's best `-ncmoe 16` holds 32 layers on the GPU; we hold 30 + 1 resident in the streaming memory,
  which keeps a whole layer for prefill streaming. Not changed.
* **The GPU part of the step** (Coder-Next: 29 launches per layer at ~2-4 µs, the q8 quantizations of the activations, two L2 norms, a tile
  and a sigmoid among them; the 122B's 8.6 ms): kernel fusion in the shader lowering is the next lever for both models; not started.

### 70.2 Decode attention: no combine where no row splits, the split count from the key count

The split-K decode attention (`decode` in attention.slang) splits a row's keys into ranges of at least `DEC_MIN_KEYS` keys, up to a
count set by the workgroup target (`DEC_TARGET_WG` / (rows x groups)), and `decode_combine` merges the ranges' partials. Two things
cost time at decode batch sizes:

* **Combine launches that merge nothing.** The combine was launched whenever the decode kernel ran, and returned for rows of one range.
  Now it is launched only when the launch can split a row (`DecodeAttentionPlan.Combines`): not where the target allows one range per
  row (Qwen3-8B-FP8 at 64 rows: 512 / (64 x 8) = 1, all 36 layers), and not for sliding-window layers whose window fits one range
  (`SingleRange`: gpt-oss's 128-key window against 256-key ranges, 12 of 24 layers; their grid also drops to one range). Exact: the
  kernel writes those rows directly either way. Combine launches per 20 steps: gpt-oss-20b 480 → 240, Qwen3-8B-FP8 720 → 0 at 64 rows.
* **A short last range.** The range length was the even split rounded up to `DEC_MIN_KEYS`, so gpt-oss's full-attention layers at
  ~300 keys ran two ranges of 256 and ~44 keys at 64 rows (twice the workgroups, a near-empty second one, and the combine). Now the
  count is the number of `DEC_MIN_KEYS` ranges the row fills (rounded down), at most the target's, with the keys spread evenly: one
  range of 320 keys at 64 rows. Where a launch has few workgroups (rows x groups x ranges under an eighth of the target) the count is
  rounded up instead: there each range's latency, not the work, sets the time, and rounding down had cost one Qwen3-8B-FP8 row at
  ~280 keys 11.33 → 11.40 ms per step (two ranges instead of three); rounded up and evened it is 11.23 (`steps/v2_*`, `steps/v3_*`).
  Ranges stay multiples of the batch (`DEC_BC`); single rows at 1000-3000 keys keep their old count and lengths (13 x 256 keys at 3,100).

Alternated pairs on the way (GPU ms, `--text`, min of 20; `steps/`):

| step | before | combine skipped (A) | + round down (B) | + few-workgroup round up (final) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| gpt-oss-20b, 64 sequences | 18.86 / 18.95 | 18.88 | 18.68 / 18.73 | (70.1) |
| gpt-oss-20b, 64 sequences (another session) | 18.39 / 18.39 | | 18.13 | 18.18 |
| Qwen3-8B-FP8, 1 sequence | 11.33 / 11.32 | | 11.40 / 11.39 | 11.23 / 11.22 |
| Qwen3-8B-FP8, 64 sequences | 16.16 / 16.27 | 16.12 / 16.08 | 16.13 | (70.1) |

`StatefulTests.CachedAttentionFewLongRows` (new: 2-4 decode rows over ~3,000 keys with 128 KV heads, several ranges per row, against the
CPU) and the attention test classes cover the new split.

### 70.3 The expert GEMM's activation copies are not where the energy goes (lever 1)

§68.7's first lever was the activation traffic of the grouped MXFP4 GEMM's 32-row decode tiles (each column block copies its expert's
rows again). Its bound, measured first: the sustained replay of §67.2 (216 real-text routings of 64-sequence steps over 24 weight
copies, `bench/s56_moe`, ms per layer; `harness/expert_tiles_sustained.txt`):

| gate / up (dual, N 2880) | sustained | isolated | | down (N 2880) | sustained | isolated |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|---:|---:|
| `develop`: 128 weight rows, 4 stages, 2 blocks / SM | 0.347-0.355 | 0.322-0.324 | | 192 rows, 4 stages, 2 blocks | 0.176-0.180 | 0.170 |
| no activation copies after the ring fill (`NM_NOA`, wrong products: the bound) | 0.346-0.352 | 0.319-0.320 | | | 0.174-0.175 | 0.168 |
| 256 weight rows (half the activation copies per weight), 3 stages, 2 blocks | 0.362 | 0.341 | | 320 rows, 3 stages | 0.197 | 0.188 |
| 128 rows, 5 stages | 0.364-0.369 | 0.324-0.325 | | 128 rows, 5 stages | 0.181-0.182 | 0.172 |
| 128 rows, 4 stages, 3 blocks / SM (`__launch_bounds__`) | 0.353-0.359 | 0.323-0.324 | | 192 rows, 3 stages, 3 blocks | 0.184-0.185 | 0.173 |
| 128 rows, 3 stages, 2 blocks | 0.375 | 0.344 | | 128 rows, 4 stages, 3 blocks | 0.180-0.181 | 0.173 |

Removing every activation copy saves 0.5-2 %: the activation rows of a decode tile (~9.5 items per expert at 64 sequences) are a fifth
of the copied bytes and hit L2. Wider column tiles halve them but lose more to fewer blocks in flight (three stages to fit two blocks)
and the last-wave tail; a cluster-shared activation tile would at best reach the `NM_NOA` row. The current tile (128 rows, four stages,
two blocks) is the best of these; the gap to Marlin (12.7 against 11.4 ms per step) is not in the activation traffic. Not built.

### 70.4 What did not work

* **The router's logits in its top-k launch** (lever 2, `router_topk`: one workgroup per row computes the 32 logits from the f32 norm
  output, rounding x to f16 as the GEMM's copy does, 32 independent 16-byte weight loads per thread, a reduce-scatter over the subgroup,
  then `topk_softmax`'s selection; 9-128 rows, the GEMM path beyond, `SELECTED_SOFTMAX` and softmax-first routers, f16 / bf16 weights):
  correct (TopK tests against the CPU at 4 / 16 / 64 / 200 rows on both providers) and 72 launches fewer per 64-sequence step, the
  kernel 8.8-9.2 µs against 13.5 µs for the four launches' minimum times, but the step did not move: 18.20-18.21 against 18.21-18.27 ms
  (CUDA, two alternated pairs), 20.69-20.91 against 20.63-20.85 ms (Vulkan) (`rejected/ab4_*`, `rejected/vk_*`). 1 / 2 / 4 rows per
  workgroup: 9.1 / 8.8 / 11.2 µs. Withdrawn; the cheaper half, the norm writing the router's f16 copy up to 64 rows (§68.7 item 2's
  exact form, as `HalfCopies` does below 17 rows), measured 18.19 against 18.20-18.22 ms (`rejected/nhc_*`): not kept either.
* **The o projection's f16 copy from the attention combine** (lever 3): the copy is row-ranged (`f16_range_scale`: the scale needs the
  row's maximum over all 64 heads), and a row's heads are written by eight decode workgroups (or the combine), so no writer sees a row.
  Not attempted; the copy is 2.8 µs per layer.
* **Qwen3 FP8 at 64 rows on two blocks per SM** (lever 4): a 64 x 64 tile in three stages needs 50.7 KB, two of them 103.4 KB with the
  per-block reserve, above the SM's 100 KB. The 32-row token tile (three stages, two blocks per SM, two token tiles for 64 rows) in
  `bench/s57_gemm` at 64 rows: gate / up 0.146 against 0.144 ms sustained, down 0.053 against 0.043, o 0.019 against 0.015
  (`harness/fp8_token_tiles_64rows.txt`): the second read of each weight tile from L2 costs more than the second block gains.
* **Decode-attention shapes** (`rejected/wg_*`, `dr_*`, `cfg*`, `long128_*`, `rk*`): 256 threads per workgroup (twice the lane groups):
  64 sequences +1.5 % on both models, one Qwen3 row -1.2 %, gpt-oss at 32K +1-2 %; eight key rows per lane group and batch: +0.7 % at 1 / 64
  rows; two: within noise. A larger workgroup target for head size 64 (2048): 4 x 128K -1.0 % (24.58 → 24.33 ms), but 4 x 32K +1.2 % and
  16 x 4K +1.7 %; 4096: 4 x 128K -1.8 %, one 128K row +1.4 %. Ranges of at most 1024 keys for launches of up to 4 rows (lever 5, the grid
  sized for the cache's longest context): 4 x 32K +2.6 % (gpt-oss) / +2.3 % (Qwen3), single rows +0.6 %, and 4 x 128K unchanged
  (24.64 against 24.62 ms), unlike the 4096 target with the same 128 ranges per row; the extra grid of mostly exiting workgroups costs
  more than it gains, and why the 128K case differs is not understood. Withdrawn.

| Qwen3-8B-FP8 serving 16 / 64 streams | 0.93 / 0.92 | 16 streams: the skinny dual gate / up; 64: its decode step |
| Qwen3-8B-FP8 long prefill 128K | 0.94 | attention at head size 128 (one fragment per warp) |
| gpt-oss-20b long prefill 16K / 32K / 64K / 128K | 0.96 / 0.97 / 0.98 / 1.01 | MoE and attention at 16K-32K |
| gpt-oss-20b decode at depth 32K / 128K, 1 / 4 streams | 1.04 / 1.11, 0.99 / 0.93 | decode attention: 4 x 128K runs 4096-key ranges (70.4) |

Ranked levers:

1. **Qwen3 small launches** (~0.8 ms per 64-sequence step above vLLM's): the fused Add + RmsNorm + E4M3 kernel (7.8 µs mean, 4096-wide
   rows, scalar loads, two barriers) in vectorized form; the o / down inputs quantized by their producers (the attention combine or
   decode kernel and the gate / up epilogue); q / k norm + rope in one launch.
2. **Expert GEMM energy per weight byte** (gpt-oss, 66 % of the step): with the copies ruled out (70.3), the MMAs and the decode are
   what is left (§67.3: without MMAs -6 %, without the decode -2 %): weights as the 16-row A operand and tokens as the 8-column B
   operand halves the MMAs of tiles of up to 8 items (most decode tiles at 64 sequences), with the decoded weights in A-fragment layout.
3. **Decode attention at short contexts** (gpt-oss 1.41 against 1.18 ms per step): latency-bound at 512 workgroups (256 threads or more
   rows per batch lose, 70.4); a tensor-core GQA decode (the 8 query heads of a KV head as the M rows of m16n8k16) cuts the score and
   P·V instructions.
4. **Few long rows** (4 x 128K, 0.93x): ranges of ~1024 keys help when the grid does not carry mostly exiting workgroups; needs a
   launch whose range count follows the step's longest row (a per-step grid from the decode metadata, or a persistent loop over ranges).
5. **Per-expert tile class in one launch** (§67.2): at most 0.26 ms per 64-sequence gpt-oss step.
6. **Head size 128 prefill attention** (Qwen3 128K 0.94x, §67.7 item 6).

### 71.2 Where the GPU part of the step went

At the start (§69, nsys with node-level graph traces, one Coder-Next decode step): 1349 kernels, 6.67 ms of GPU busy time. A linear-attention
layer whose experts run on the CPU had 27 launches in its GPU segment, a GPU-resident layer ~29 (879 for the 30 layers and the head). The
small ones on the critical path: the router top-k 15.2 µs per layer (one subgroup over 512 logits, its per-lane sorted lists dynamically
indexed and therefore in local memory: 0.74 ms per step), 5.3 q8_1 quantizations per layer (255 per step, 0.68 ms; the post-attention norm's
output was quantized twice in resident layers, once for the shared expert and once for the routed experts, whose launches differ in their
row range), two L2 norms and two Tile launches before the delta rule (Coder-Next's 16 key heads repeated in place for its 32 value heads,
6-7 µs serial per layer), the beta sigmoid and the decay `softplus(alpha + dt_bias) * a` (two launches after their matvecs), 428 generated
elementwise / norm launches per step in all (1.02 ms).

Now: 1004 kernels and 5.44 ms per step under nsys; segments of CPU layers 19 launches, resident layers ~21 (635 for 30 layers and the head).
Router top-k 5.6 µs (0.27 ms per step), 117 quantizations (0.25 ms; the rest are the shared and routed experts' down-projection inputs and
the split passes' GPU slots), 215 generated launches (0.55 ms); the delta rule 4.6 → 6.3 µs (it now normalizes q / k and reads the key head
itself). Without the profiler (`--bench 64`, same binary, fusions off / on): GPU 5.31 / 5.28 → 4.64 / 4.81 ms per step.

Qwen3.5-122B: the GPU segment of its 40 resident layers 1011 → 901 launches (the router top-k and the q8 quantizations behind its norms),
CPU-layer segments 23 → 21; its GPU time per step stayed at 8.5-8.9 ms (fusions off in the same hour: 8.89; §69: 8.62). Its step is the
bandwidth of its matvecs (per-launch profile: the [3072 → 12288] / [3072 → 8192] / [8192 → 3072] projections at 25-36 µs and the IQ2_XXS /
IQ2_S expert matvecs at 15-21 µs are 60 % of it); its q / k need no repeat (the L2 norms were already absorbed), and its beta / alpha
projections are Q8_0, which take the f32 matvec at one row (Q8_0's int-dot range starts at 2 rows), so their gates keep their two
launches (1.6 + 1.8 µs per linear-attention layer).

The CPU side is as in §69 (CPU passes 0.30-0.35 ms per layer on a quiet minute, 0.5-0.6 ms on a busy one); llama.cpp under nsys spends a
similar ~5.6 ms per token off the GPU for 16 CPU layers, its GPU part is longer than ours (354 `mul_mat_vec_q` and as many `quantize_q8_1`
launches per token: llama.cpp quantizes the activations for every matvec).

### 71.3 Changes

* **Router top-k with the row in registers** (`topk_softmax`, `ROW_SLOTS`): a router row of a multiple of the subgroup size and up to 32
  values per lane stays in statically indexed registers (the softmax sums in the same order as before), and the K picks are subgroup argmax
  rounds over each lane's best untaken slot (key descending, index ascending: the order of the per-lane lists, so the same experts and
  weights). 512 logits / top 10 on Blackwell: 15.2 → 5.6 µs. Every MoE router of that form takes it (Qwen3.5 / 3.6 / Next: 256-512 experts;
  gpt-oss's top-k-then-softmax). `SHARPLIGHT_NO_TOPK_REGISTER_ROW=1` restores the lists.
* **Repeated key heads read in place by the delta rule** (`GROUPED_HEADS`, `KEY_HEAD(h)` in state16.slang): q / k heads repeated in place for
  grouped value heads (Reshape to [T, H, 1, D], Tile by [1, 1, R, 1], Reshape back) are recognized at the delta rule's unit; the kernel (and
  the chunked prefill form) reads key head h / R of the source, and the L2 norms behind the repeat are absorbed as they were without it:
  four launches fewer per linear-attention layer, and the chunked form's q / k preparation runs over 16 instead of 32 heads.
  `SHARPLIGHT_NO_GROUPED_KEY_HEADS=1`.
* **Row norms write the q8_1 rows of the int-dot matvecs that read them** (`RowNormKernelSource.Q8Output`): for decode steps (up to 8 rows,
  the K-quants' int-dot range) a row norm whose output an int-dot matvec reads (dense or expert; an f32 reader such as the router reads the
  f32 rows) writes the q8_1 rows next to the f32 ones, passing the row through shared memory so that eight lanes quantize 32 consecutive
  values with quantize_q8_1's arithmetic (the same bytes). Readers with a larger range (Q8_0 to 16 rows) quantize the larger steps into the
  same rows. A per-head norm read as [T, heads * D] (the gated output norm of linear attention) writes its head's part of each row. Three
  quantizations per layer fewer, in every model whose norms feed int-dot matvecs (any K-quant or block-format GGUF decode).
  `SHARPLIGHT_NO_NORM_Q8_COPY=1`.
* **Elementwise groups in the int-dot matvec's store** (`MM_EPI` for `mmvq`, the epilogue helpers now in mm_epi.slang for both kernel files):
  a plain group that reads one matmul of int-dot weights plus up to three scalars, row vectors or output-shaped tensors (the beta sigmoid,
  the decay chain with its two [32] vectors, an activation after a quantized projection, a residual add) runs in the matvec's store for
  the int-dot rows; other row counts run the matmul and the group's launch. `SHARPLIGHT_NO_INT_DOT_EPILOGUE=1`.
* Tests: `TopKTests.Router` at 512 / 1024 experts and a non-multiple of the subgroup, `TopKTests.RouterTies` (heavy ties, both router
  orders), `FusionTests.RepeatedKeyHeadsInDeltaRule` (with and without the norms, decode rows and a chunked prefill step),
  `FusionTests.NormQuantizedForIntDot` (q4_k / q8_0, 1-16 rows), `FusionTests.IntDotMatvecEpilogue`.

### 71.4 What did not work or was not done

* **Held submissions** (CUDA, reverted): the GPU segment after a CPU layer submitted before the CPU pass, its stream held by
  `cuStreamWaitValue32` on a page-locked word the host writes once the CPU's outputs are staged. No gain: the submission (~0.03 ms) ran on the
  main thread right before the CPU pass instead of beside it ("before the CPU" 0.002 → 0.045 ms), and the GPU saw the host's write ~20 µs
  late (the segment's wait 0.066 → 0.093 ms for the same 0.075 ms of device time). Holding a step while it was still being recorded or
  captured (its first two runs) hung the stream; overlapping the submission would need it on another thread, and the release latency a
  device-side flag.
* **A margin for the CPU alone in the split balancer**: in one pair of interleaved rounds Coder-Next's CPU-only passes
  (`SHARPLIGHT_SPARSE_GPU_SLOTS=0`) gave medians of 89.5 / 89.8 against 78 / 76 with the measured split; in the next pair the order reversed
  (84.8 / 72.9 against 88.9 / 78.6). The pod's noise decides; the balancer is unchanged. Qwen3.5-122B's split stays well ahead (78.5 / 78.0
  against 65.2 / 58.4 CPU-only); gpt-oss-120b is level (50.1 / 45.6 split, 51.8 / 48.8 CPU-only).
* **One layer fewer on the CPU** for Coder-Next: the placement is the same 80 GPU groups at `--batch 512`, 256 and 128 (the activations are
  not what keeps the 32nd layer off; the streaming memory, one layer's experts, is). Not changed.
* The 122B's beta / alpha gates: the store epilogue covers the int-dot matvec only, not the f32 split-K matvec its Q8_0 projections take at
  one row (~0.12 ms per step, ~1.4 %).
* Still separate launches on Coder-Next's decode path: the shared and routed experts' down-projection inputs (the dual matvec's epilogue
  output, quantized by its own launch), the shared-expert gate (an f32 [2048 → 1] matvec, its sigmoid in the next group only for resident
  layers), the conv1d.
* One 122B load at `--bench 512` ran out of device memory at its weights while another agent's server held a CUDA context (59 MiB) outside
  the GPU lock: the placement leaves too little slack for that; the same load passed on the free GPU.
* Not measured: Qwen3-8B-FP8's fused norm + FP8 activation quantization at serving batches (§70's list); the same norm machinery writes it
  (`Fp8Output`), its shared-memory reads of four values per thread are bank-conflicted 4-way.

### 72.2 Decode attention on tensor cores (lever 2 of §70.6)

At 64 sequences gpt-oss's decode attention took 1.32 ms per step against vLLM's 1.20 (`kernel_mha`, 0.70 ms for the 12 full layers and
0.50 for the 12 window layers) and far from the read bound: a full layer reads ~39 MB of keys and values (64 rows x ~300 keys x 8 KV
heads x 128 values x 2 bytes x 2) in ~74 µs (~530 GB/s; vLLM 58.6 µs), a window layer 16.8 MB in 34.8 µs (vLLM 41.6). `decode` runs each
(KV group, row, range) as 128 threads that keep 8 heads' f32 queries and accumulators per lane (~180 registers), so about two
workgroups share an SM and the 512 workgroups of a 64-row layer run in ~3 waves of scalar FMAs and shuffles.

`attn_decode_native.cu` (docs/cuda.md) keeps `decode`'s grid, split rule (`decode_split_keys`, mirrored) and partials and computes on
tensor cores: the HPW <= 8 heads of a block are the 16 rows of `mma.sync.m16n8k16` (half of them zero), each of 4 warps takes every
fourth tile of 32 keys (16 at head size 128) with its own online softmax, and nothing goes through shared memory before the final merge
of the warps: lane group g loads key / value rows g, g + 8, .. in 16-byte chunks that are used as B operands directly (the head
dimensions are permuted alike in Q and K, so the dot products are unchanged), the score accumulators are packed to f16 as the A
operands of P · V, and the value words become B operands through `movmatrix.trans` (the output columns come out in the matching
permutation, undone at the store). 111 registers at head size 64, 150 at 128, no spills. Launch-level (profile of 20 steps of 64
sequences, `steps/gptoss_profile_64_nd_prof_*`): attention 26.49 → 20.56 ms (1.32 → 1.03 ms per step), combine 1.91 → 1.79 ms.

Decode steps, GPU ms, two alternated pairs (`steps/ab_native_decode.txt`):

| step | before | after | |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| gpt-oss-20b `--text`, 1 / 16 / 32 / 48 / 64 sequences | 5.35 / 12.63-12.66 / 16.29-16.32 / 18.05-18.06 / 18.72-18.82 | 5.25-5.26 / 12.57-12.59 / 16.12-16.15 / 17.72-17.85 / 18.42-18.44 | -1.8 / -0.5 / -1.0 / -1.5 / -1.9 % |
| gpt-oss-20b `--feedback`, 16 / 64 sequences | 9.93-9.95 / 16.83-16.86 | 9.88 / 16.51-16.53 | -0.6 / -1.9 % |
| Qwen3-8B-FP8 `--text`, 1 / 8 / 16 / 32 / 48 / 64 | 11.23-11.24 / 12.74-12.75 / 12.85-12.87 / 13.73 / 15.36 / 16.37-16.38 | 11.17-11.18 / 12.62-12.74 / 12.84-12.85 / 13.65 / 15.08-15.09 / 16.36 | -0.5 / -0.5 / 0 / -0.6 / -1.8 / 0 % |
| gpt-oss-20b at depth 32K, 1 / 4 streams | 6.39 / 11.57 | 6.26 / 11.46 | -2.0 / -1.0 % |
| gpt-oss-20b at depth 128K, 1 / 4 streams | 9.42 / 24.64 | 9.29 / 24.06 | -1.4 / -2.4 % |
| Qwen3-8B-FP8 at depth 32K, 1 / 4 streams | 17.17 / 36.21 | 17.03 / 36.01 | -0.8 / -0.6 % |

(Depth: BatchBench as `s58_long.sh` runs it, `--slots 4 --depth D --batch 2048 --sizes 1,4 --reps 5`, `long/`.) Qwen3-8B-FP8 runs 4 heads
per block (12 of 16 MMA rows empty) and at 64 rows a single 300-key range per (row, group), where both kernels are close to their
latency floor; its 48-row steps gain. At 128K the 4-stream step reads 12.9 GB of cache per step in 17.1 ms (`decode`: ~760 GB/s, the
profile in `long/gptoss_128k_4_profile_fixed_ids.txt`), so the gain there is the last few percent of the read rate.

Groups narrow enough for the fused combine (heads per block x head size <= 256, e.g. 4 x 64) keep `decode`: their last workgroup merges
the partials, which this kernel does not do. Tests: `StatefulTests.CachedAttentionGroupedDecode` (new; head sizes 64 / 128, 2-8 heads per
block, ~3,000-key rows in several ranges and in one), `CachedAttentionSinks` with 16 query heads (full and windowed), and
`PagedAttentionMatchesCpu` with 16 / 2 and 16 / 4 heads (multi-sequence, paged): each fails with the kernel's output halved, which the
previous cases did not (only `CachedAttentionLongPrefill`'s f16 / 128 / 8 / 2 case reached it).

### 72.3 The expert GEMM's operand swap (lever 1 of the brief, §70.6 item 2) and a contiguous weight layout: measured, not kept

* **Weights as the 16-row A operand, tokens as the 8-column B operand** (`NM_SWAP`, `rejected/moe_operand_swap.diff`): the decoded
  B-layout fragments of two 8-row units are exactly an A fragment (rows g and g + 8), the token rows one `ldmatrix.x4` per 8 rows and
  32-value block, so a tile's MMAs and activation `ldmatrix` bytes follow its items in steps of 8 instead of 16. On the text routing of
  §67.2 63 % of the 64-sequence step's 32-row tiles hold at most 8 items (3,833 of 6,121; 1,251 hold 9-16), so the swap removes ~40 % of
  the decode tiles' MMAs; products identical to the reference (same maximum errors at 32-512 tokens). Sustained replay (216 routings over
  24 weight copies, ms per layer, `rejected/swap_harness_run*.txt`):

  | | `develop` | swapped, one accumulator chain | swapped, one accumulator set per 16-value half | no MMAs at all (wrong products: the bound) |
  |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
  | gate / up (dual, 128 weight rows) | 0.352-0.360 | 0.349-0.357 | 0.351-0.352 | 0.312-0.315 |
  | down (192 rows) | 0.177-0.178 | 0.182-0.183 | 0.181-0.182 | |
  | down (128 rows) | 0.179 | 0.180 | 0.180 | |

  With one (token, weight) fragment pair per warp the swapped MMAs form a single dependent chain; two chains bring gate / up to -2 % in
  the harness, but in the engine the gate / up launches summed 165.8 → 166.5 ms over 20 steps and the step was unchanged (17.29-17.35 /
  17.32-17.36 ms, `rejected/swap_step_*`), and the down product loses where its 24-row warp tiles leave half an A fragment empty.
  Halving the MMAs of most tiles does not buy what removing all of them would (-11 %): the decode tiles are not issue-bound on the
  tensor pipe. Withdrawn.
* **A contiguous weight layout per column tile** (timing only: each column tile's 128 x 32 bytes of a K step stored contiguously, as a
  Marlin-style repack would; `rejected/contig_layout_harness.txt`): gate / up 0.355-0.357 → 0.365, down 0.178 → 0.188 ms per layer. The
  current row-strided reads with 256-byte L2 prefetches stream better than one 4 KB block per K step; Marlin's advantage
  (11.25 against our 12.7 ms per step, ~790 against ~700 GB/s effective) is not its layout. Not pursued.

### 72.4 Few long rows (lever 3): the gap is outside attention

At 4 x 128K the decode attention reads 12.9 GB per step at ~760 GB/s already (17.06 ms of the 24.65 ms step; 72.2 takes it to ~16.5).
vLLM's 174.9 tok/s (22.9 ms per step) cannot come from a faster attention at the same bytes; the rest of our step (~7.5 ms: expert
GEMMs 3.7, LM head 1.4, projections ~1.6) is where vLLM is ahead. The comparison was also not like for like: `s58_long_vllm.py` lets
vLLM generate from random-token prompts (its routing follows the generated tokens), while BatchBench without `--feedback` repeats fixed
ids. With `--feedback` our 4 x 128K step is 25.03 ms (24.65 with fixed ids): the expert GEMMs take 5.1 instead of 3.7 ms
(`long/gptoss_128k_4_profile_*`), so like for like the point is ~0.91x before this round (~0.93x after). Sizing the launch by the longest row (lever 3 as briefed) was not built:
the attention it would shorten is at the read rate.

### 72.5 Correctness and tests

* Greedy text, 120 tokens, CUDA, the prompts of §65 / §70 (~40 / ~1000 / ~3000 words), native decode off against on (`greedy/`):
  Qwen3-8B-FP8 byte-identical on all three, gpt-oss-20b on ~40 and ~1000; at ~3000 the first heading flips between "**Historical
  Overview**" (before) and "**Historical Context**" (after), the near-tie §65.6 measured (" Context" 19.323 / " Overview" 19.286):
  the kernel rounds Q · SCALE and the probabilities to f16 as the prefill kernel does.
* Sharplight.Cuda.Tests: 39 / 0 failed / 1 skipped (cuBLASLt). Sharplight.Vulkan.Tests, one process per class (Moe, StreamedExperts,
  MatMul, Fusion, RowInvariance, TopK, FullAttention, PagedAttention, PackedSequence, SparseAttention, Stateful, StateHandoff,
  CompressedKv): CUDA provider 622 / 0 failed / 0 skipped, Vulkan provider 622 / 0 failed / 0 skipped (`tests/tests.txt`), with the new
  cases of 72.2.
* Vulkan: no Vulkan code changed (the kernel is CUDA C++ behind `native_attention`); gpt-oss-20b on the Vulkan provider, `--text`, 1 / 16 / 64 sequences: 5.29 / 12.88 / 20.88 ms
  (§70: 5.28-5.29 / 12.92-12.93 / 21.13-21.27; `vulkan/`).

### 72.6 Gap to vLLM and plan (state after this round)

| benchmark | CUDA / vLLM | where the time goes |
|---|---:|---|
| gpt-oss-20b decode step, 64 sequences (`--text` / `--feedback`) | 0.99 / 0.99 (16.93 against 16.8 ms in the same hold) | expert GEMMs ~12.7 against Marlin's 11.25 ms; attention 1.03 against 1.20 (now ahead); q / k / v + o, routing and small launches |
| Qwen3-8B-FP8 decode step, 64 sequences | 0.96-0.99 (clock-dependent; 16.36 / 15.76 against 15.64 ms) | norms with the FP8 quantization, q / k norm + rope, the o / down inputs' quantization (perf/offload-r5) |
| gpt-oss-20b serving 16 / 64 streams | 0.95 / 0.92 | prompt waves on full expert tiles, decode steps as above |
| Qwen3-8B-FP8 serving 16 / 64 streams | 0.94 / 0.93 | 16 streams: the skinny dual gate / up; 64: its decode step |
| gpt-oss-20b long prefill 16K-128K | 0.96 / 0.97 / 0.99 / 1.01 | MoE and attention at 16K-32K |
| gpt-oss-20b decode at depth 32K / 128K, 1 / 4 streams | 1.06 / 1.12, 1.00 / 0.95 | 4 x 128K: attention at the read rate; the expert GEMMs at 4 rows (fed-back routing, 72.4), the LM head |
| Qwen3-8B-FP8 long prefill 128K | 0.94 | attention at head size 128 |

Ranked levers:

1. **Expert GEMM per-byte efficiency** (gpt-oss, ~12.7 against Marlin's 11.25 ms per 64-sequence step): neither the activation copies
   (§70.3), the MMA count (72.3) nor the weight layout (72.3) is it; what is left is the decode arithmetic and the clocks under the power
   cap. Next measurement: the harness with the decode replaced by a constant (MMAs kept) under sustained replay, and SM clocks sampled
   during both kernels (vLLM's Marlin against ours) to see whether ours runs at a lower clock for the same bytes.
2. **Qwen3 small launches** (perf/offload-r5's fusions; ~0.8 ms per 64-sequence step above vLLM's).
3. **The rest of the long-context step** (4 x 128K 0.93x): the expert GEMMs at 4 rows on fed-back routing (5.1 ms per step, skinny
   GEMM), the LM head (1.4 ms at the read limit); make `s58_long.sh`'s decode points use `--feedback` (like for like with vLLM).
4. **Fused combine in `attn_decode_native.cu`** for narrow groups (models with 1-4 heads per KV head at head size 64-128 keep `decode`).
5. **Per-expert tile class in one launch** (§67.2): at most 0.26 ms per 64-sequence gpt-oss step.
6. **Head size 128 prefill attention** (Qwen3 128K 0.94x).

for v in 0 1; do SHARPLIGHT_NATIVE_DECODE=$v $BB ~/models/hf/gpt-oss-20b --provider cuda --slots 4 --ctx 131584 --depth 131072 --batch 2048 \
  --sizes 1,4 --modes greedy --reps 5; done   # add --feedback for vLLM's routing
python bench/s54_vllm_decode_profile.py ~/models/hf/gpt-oss-20b --seqs 64 --words

## 73. LLM round 23: the expert GEMM against Marlin on the same routing, at the power limit; like-for-like decode baselines (2026-11-21)

Branch `perf/llm-r23` (base `develop` at `776eaf04`, round 22 merged). GPU 0 of the RunPod machine (RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell, 82 SMs,
200 W cap, performance counters blocked), shared with other agents: every timed run held the verify lock, variants alternated in the same
hold, one disturbed hold (another process allocated 26.7 GB during it) discarded. vLLM 0.33.0 (§56's CUDA build), its profiles and the
long-context runs inside the final measurements' hold. This round changes no engine code: it measures where the expert GEMM's gap to
Marlin is (lever 1 of §72.6), rejects six kernel variants, and makes the long-context decode points like for like (lever 3). Raw
output in [`bench/results/s73/`](../bench/results/s73).

New tools: `bench/s73_clock_sampler.py` (NVML SM / memory clock, power, temperature and clock-event reasons every 2 ms while a command
runs), `bench/s73_marlin_replay.py` (vLLM's `moe_wna16_marlin_gemm` on recorded routings, 24 weight copies, one CUDA graph, in vLLM's
padded gpt-oss shapes: hidden 3072, intermediate 2944, 9 % more weight bytes than the checkpoint's 2880), `bench/s73_vllm_routing.py`
(vLLM's own decode routing as a routing file), `SUSTAINED_ONLY` / `PER_ROUTE` in `bench/s56_moe`, `--skip N` in
`s54_vllm_decode_profile.py`, and `s58_long.sh` decode points with `--feedback` (`DECODE_ARGS`).

### 73.1 Against vLLM (final hold; same build before and after: what changed is the accounting)

| benchmark (CUDA) | Sharplight | vLLM | ours / vLLM (§72 → like for like) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| gpt-oss-20b decode step, 64 sequences, `--text` (GPU ms; vLLM profile + 1.6 ms LM head and sampling, §64) | 17.71-17.79 (two runs) | 15.25 + 1.6 = 16.85 (all 61 steps), 15.53 + 1.6 = 17.13 (steps 6-61) | 0.99 → 0.95-0.96 (this hold) |
| gpt-oss-20b decode step, 64 sequences, `--feedback` | 16.42-16.45 | 16.3 (§64, random-token prompts) | 0.99 |
| gpt-oss-20b decode step, 1 / 16 sequences, `--text` | 5.26 / 12.56-12.59 | | (§72: 5.25 / 12.57) |
| Qwen3-8B-FP8 decode step, 64 sequences, `--text` | 15.87 (two runs) | 14.08 + 1.55 = 15.63 | 0.96-0.99 → 0.98 |
| gpt-oss-20b prefill 16K / 32K / 64K / 128K (tok/s, median of 5) | 13,900 / 12,005 / 9,378 / 6,505 | 14,509 / 12,301 / 9,423 / 6,423 | 0.96 / 0.98 / 1.00 / 1.01 |
| gpt-oss-20b decode at depth 32K, 1 / 4 streams, **fed back** (tok/s from the GPU ms) | 160.3 / 323.4 (6.24 / 12.37 ms) | 151.4 / 307.6 | 1.06 / 1.12 (fixed ids) → **1.06 / 1.05** |
| gpt-oss-20b decode at depth 128K, 1 / 4 streams, **fed back** | 107.5 / 163.5 (9.30 / 24.47 ms) | 107.3 / 174.9 (§64; this session's run hit a device assert past 131,072 positions) | 1.00 / 0.95 → **1.00 / 0.93** |
| gpt-oss-20b / Qwen3-8B-FP8 serving 16 / 64 streams | unchanged code (§72: 0.95 / 0.92, 0.94 / 0.93) | | |
| Qwen3-8B-FP8 prefill 128K | unchanged code (§70: 2,477 tok/s) | 2,639 | 0.94 |

* Steps: BatchBench `--slots 64 --ctx 640 --depth 256 --sizes 1,16,64 --modes greedy --reps 20`, GPU ms (min of 20, after 5 warm-up
  steps), two runs alternated with the vLLM profiles (`final/steps/`, `final/vllm/`). The `--text` step moves between holds by more than
  vLLM's does (17.75, 18.72-18.82, 16.93 in §72's three holds, 17.71-17.79 here, with vLLM at 15.19-15.25 each time); `--feedback`
  measured 16.42-16.45 here against 16.51-16.53 in §72.
* vLLM's decode steps get slower as its generations go on: its random-word prompts end in repetition loops (50 distinct generations of 64,
  the most common " hand hand hand ..."), and its routing is most concentrated right after the prefill (73.3). Averaged over steps
  1-61 the step is 15.25 ms, over 6-61 15.53, over 21-61 15.94 (§72's trace: 15.19 / 15.49 / 15.94). BatchBench's min after five
  warm-up steps compares with the 6-61 figure at the least, so §72's 0.99x was slightly pessimistic for us (and this hold's `--text`
  run slightly slow). `s54_vllm_decode_profile.py --skip 5` prints it.
* Depth (`final/long/`): `s58_long.sh` with the new default `DECODE_ARGS=--feedback`, i.e. the fed-back routing of 72.4 and of vLLM's
  generated tokens. At 32K the 4-stream point drops from 1.12x (fixed ids, §72) to 1.05x like for like: 12.37 against 11.46 ms per step,
  the expert GEMMs reading more experts per step. At 128K, 4 streams: 0.93x, as 72.4 estimated.

### 73.2 Clocks and power: both kernels run at the power limit, Marlin at a higher SM clock

The sustained replay of §67.2 (216 text routings of 64-sequence steps over 24 weight copies, ms per layer), sampled with
`s73_clock_sampler.py` (medians over the busy window; clock-event reason 0x4 = software power cap, share of samples;
`harness/clocks_r2.summary.txt`, two passes each):

| kernel | ms per layer | SM clock | board power | power cap active |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Marlin gate / up (padded, 5888 x 3072 per expert) | 0.3385-0.3408 | 2017-2047 MHz | 200.0 W | 87-90 % |
| ours gate / up (5760 x 2880) | 0.3455-0.3486 | 1732-1740 MHz | 187-189 W | 100 % |
| Marlin down (padded) | 0.1740-0.1746 | 2047-2070 MHz | 200.0 W | 92 % |
| ours down | 0.1766 | 1822-1830 MHz | 186-187 W | 86-100 % |
| ours gate / up without the decode and the MMAs (copies only, `skel`) | 0.3132-0.3136 (r1) | 1695-1702 MHz | 146-147 W | 92 % |

Ours runs ~300 MHz lower than Marlin and is held there by the power limiter, although the board draws 11-13 W less than the cap; even the
copy-only skeleton at 147 W is power-capped at 1.7 GHz. So the limiter reacts to something other than the averaged board power NVML
reports (a rail or a faster power estimate it does not break out), and the SM clock is not what bounds the kernel: variants that cost
fewer SM instructions ran at a *higher* clock and were *slower* (73.4). Marlin, reading 9 % more bytes, takes 2 % less time per layer
than ours on this routing (0.513 against 0.524 ms); per weight byte it is ~10 % more efficient.

### 73.3 Same routing for both: vLLM's own routing touches 11 % fewer experts

`s73_vllm_routing.py` records vLLM's routing behind its decode-step profile (`--words` workload, 61 steps x 24 layers,
`routing/vllm64_words.txt`): **24.2 experts touched per layer**, against 27.2 in our BatchBench `--text` routing (§67.2); 16.3 at the
first decode step, 20.3 at step 7, 24-26.5 from step 13 on. Both kernels on both routings in one hold (`harness/clocks_r3.summary.txt`,
sustained, ms per layer, gate / up + down):

| routing | ours | Marlin (padded) | ours / Marlin |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| ours (`--text`, 27.2 experts, 28.3 32-row tiles per layer) | 0.339-0.353 + 0.173-0.177 = 0.521 | 0.340-0.348 + 0.174 = 0.518 | 1.01 |
| vLLM's (24.2 experts, 26.5 tiles, 2.27 experts with more than 32 items) | 0.339-0.340 + 0.173-0.177 = 0.514 | 0.309-0.310 + 0.158-0.159 = 0.468 | 1.10 |

Marlin's time follows the bytes (-10 %); ours moves 1.3 %. Isolated launches show why (`harness/perroute_*.txt`): our time is linear in
the routing tiles, 11.1 µs per gate / up tile and 5.9 µs per down tile, with no steps at wave boundaries (so the grid's wave quantization
is not it), and an expert with more than 32 items costs a second full tile. Cutting those tiles to 32 rows (`CLAMP=1`) leaves the time
unchanged (0.3384-0.3394), so their second read is not the cost either: on vLLM's routing the extra tiles' work (MMAs, decode, copies of
the extra blocks) is what Marlin does not pay, as its blocks take up to 64 rows of an expert in one pass. Inside vLLM's step Marlin takes
11.29 ms (all steps) to 11.99 ms (steps 21-61) per step; in our step the expert GEMMs take ~12.6 ms (24 x 0.524).

### 73.4 Kernel variants measured, not kept

Sustained replay as 73.2 / 73.3, ms per layer, all alternated with `develop` in the same hold (`rejected/moe_diag_variants.diff` holds the
diagnostic switches; `harness/clocks_r*.summary.txt`):

| variant | gate / up (ours / vLLM routing) | down | note |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `develop` | 0.345-0.352 / 0.338-0.341 | 0.175-0.177 | |
| `develop`, first hold (r1, ours routing; the four rows below are from it) | 0.337-0.351 | 0.172-0.180 | 189 W, 1732 MHz |
| decode replaced by constant B fragments (`NM_DIAG=1`, wrong products: the decode's cost) | 0.317-0.322 | 0.164-0.166 | 157 W, 1702 MHz |
| codes loaded, no decode arithmetic (`NM_DIAG=2`) | 0.333-0.334 | 0.169 | 182 W |
| no MMAs (`NM_NOMMA`) | 0.328-0.335 | 0.168-0.169 | 177 W |
| neither (copies only, `skel`) | 0.313-0.314 | 0.161 | 147 W, 1695 MHz |
| no L2 prefetch hint on the weight copies (`NM_PF=0`) | 0.696 | 0.372 | 2.6 GHz, 200 W: the hint is the DRAM efficiency |
| 128-byte hint | 0.345-0.351 | 0.176 | same |
| the 256-byte hint on the first 16 bytes of each 256-byte block only (`NM_PF=1`), and with the next block prefetched (`NM_PF=2`) | 0.481-0.483 | 0.258 | 2.2 GHz at 200 W |
| E8M0 factors made with one integer multiply-add (exact for bytes 99-128, others behind a warp vote; no 1 KB table) | 0.356 / 0.345-0.346 | 0.179-0.180 | fewer instructions, higher clock (1.79-1.83 GHz, 196-200 W), slower |
| 64-row routing tiles (each expert read once up to 64 items; four stages without the table) | 0.368-0.370 / 0.350 | 0.185-0.186 / 0.180 | per tile 14.2 against 12.8 µs; twice the loop code |
| the same with the integer factors | 0.362-0.370 / 0.344-0.345 | 0.187-0.188 / 0.183 | |
| rows past a partial tile zeroed once in every stage, so the MMAs multiply zeros (`NM_ZERO`) | 0.340-0.345 / 0.338-0.339 | 0.174-0.175 | -0.3-1.2 %, 1-2 W less: within a step's noise |

Products checked against the harness's reference for every variant that keeps them (32-2048 tokens; E8M0 bytes 120-127, 126-133 and
94-101 for the integer factors' slow path). The decode is ~7 % of the sustained gate / up time and the MMAs ~4 %; the copies
with their 256-byte L2 prefetch hints are the rest, and the hints decide the DRAM efficiency (without them 2x slower). The integer
factors confirm 73.2: a variant that frees SM issue slots raises the clock and the power and does not get faster. Per byte Marlin is
better by its memory path (contiguous 16-byte-per-thread blocks of a repacked layout, no per-copy prefetch hints), which §72.3's
contiguous-layout test could not reach because it dropped the hints' prefetch depth.

### 73.5 Correctness and tests

No engine, shader or kernel code changed (bench scripts and the harness only), so greedy output and the test suites are those of §72.5.
The harness's product checks are in 73.4.

### 73.6 Gap to vLLM and plan (state after this round)

| benchmark | CUDA / vLLM | where the time goes |
|---|---:|---|
| gpt-oss-20b decode step, 64 sequences (`--text` / `--feedback`) | 0.95-0.99 / 0.99 (hold-dependent `--text`) | expert GEMMs ~12.6 ms against Marlin's 11.3-12.0 (same kernels at par on our routing, 10 % behind on vLLM's concentrated one, 73.3) |
| Qwen3-8B-FP8 decode step, 64 sequences | 0.98 | norms with the FP8 quantization, q / k norm + rope (perf/offload-r5) |
| gpt-oss-20b serving 16 / 64 streams | 0.95 / 0.92 | prompt waves on full expert tiles, decode steps |
| gpt-oss-20b long prefill 16K-128K | 0.96 / 0.98 / 1.00 / 1.01 | MoE and attention at 16K-32K |
| gpt-oss-20b decode at depth 32K / 128K, 1 / 4 streams, fed back | 1.06 / 1.05, 1.00 / 0.93 | 4 streams: the expert GEMMs at 16 rows (skinny GEMM, near the read rate) and the LM head; 128K: attention at the read rate |
| Qwen3-8B-FP8 long prefill 128K | 0.94 | attention at head size 128 |

Ranked levers:

1. **Expert GEMM tiles of up to 64 rows at the 32-row tile's cost** (gpt-oss at 64 sequences, worth up to the 10 % of 73.3 on vLLM-like
   routing, ~0.5-1.2 ms per step): one launch where each expert takes one block row of up to 64 items. The 64-row build loses 11 % per tile
   (73.4); suspects are the twice-as-long loop (four fragment cases unrolled with the interleaved decode) and the larger activation
   stages. Next: one generic loop over live fragments instead of the unrolled switch, then a per-expert tile height inside one launch.
2. **Marlin's memory path**: a repacked weight layout read in contiguous 16-byte-per-thread blocks with an explicit deep L2 prefetch
   (bulk `cp.async.bulk.prefetch.L2` per row segment) in place of a hint on every copy; measure energy per byte with the sampler.
3. **Qwen3 small launches** (perf/offload-r5's fusions).
4. **Long-context 4-stream decode** (0.93 at 128K, 1.05 at 32K like for like): the 16-row expert GEMMs and the LM head per step.
5. **Fused combine in `attn_decode_native.cu`** for narrow groups.
6. **Head size 128 prefill attention** (Qwen3 128K 0.94x).

PY=$VLLM_VENV/bin/python; R=bench/results/s67/harness/routes64_text.txt

$PY bench/s73_vllm_routing.py ~/models/hf/gpt-oss-20b --out vllm64_words.txt
$PY bench/s73_clock_sampler.py --gpu <i> --out gu.csv -- env ROUTES=$R LAYERS=24 PASSES=80 SUSTAINED_ONLY=1 bench/s56_moe/gu_base
$PY bench/s73_clock_sampler.py --gpu <i> --out marlin.csv -- $PY bench/s73_marlin_replay.py $R --product gate_up --seconds 6
# variants: git apply bench/results/s73/rejected/moe_diag_variants.diff, build with -DNM_DIAG=1|2, -DNM_NOMMA=1, -DNM_PF=0|1|2|128,
